"Yes," she gasped, her voice raw and rough, her body pressing against Sam's, her nails raking down their back, leaving red lines in their wake. "Just like that. Harder, faster, more."

She could feel Sam's cock throbbing, pulsing, aching, desperate for release. She knew they were close, knew they were on the edge, knew they were about to come undone.

And she wanted to be there with them, wanted to feel them come, wanted to come with them, wanted to experience that ultimate, all-consuming, mind-blowing, earth-shattering, life-changing, fucking incredible moment together.

"Come for me," she demanded, her voice a low, guttural growl. "Come for me, fucking come for me, come hard, come fast, come until you can't come anymore, come until you're screaming, until you're begging, until you're fucking broken."

rows.desc: clothes off and physical initiation -- unambiguously heading into sex and stated plainly, but the act itself not yet depicted
rows.ask: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."
rows.reply:
Nadia didn’t cover herself. She stood there bare and utterly unashamed, her expression sharpening as his hands finished what they’d started. Her fingers closed around his wrist—not hard enough to hurt, but hard enough to make a point.

“You got lucky,” she said, voice low and edged. “I wanted that. Next time, wait until I say.”

She released him and stepped back, putting just enough space between them to keep the point clear.

“You asked what I like,” she said. “So listen. I like being fucked, not romanced. No kissing unless I ask. No sweet talk. No pretending this is anything but appetite.”

Her gaze flicked once to the nightstand, then back to him.

“I like it hard and deep. I like being used like I’m not something fragile. I like a hand on my throat only if I tell you it’s allowed. I like being told what you’re going to do before you do it, and I like it when you don’t waste time asking permission for things I’ve already answered.”

She crossed her arms, not modest, just impatient.

“Condom. Top drawer. Put it on, get on the bed, and keep your hands where I can see them until I tell you otherwise. If you want to touch me, ask. If I say stop, you stop. If you need to stop, you say it.”

Her chin lifted slightly.

“Now move, unless you suddenly decided you need more instructions.”

rows.desc: explicit with specific anatomical and act language
rows.ask: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.
rows.reply:
Nadia’s head tipped back against the mattress, a sharp curse leaving her before she could swallow it. Her thighs tightened around him, then forced themselves loose again, because losing control that fast irritated her. Her hand stayed fisted in his hair, holding him there while her breath broke into pieces.

She let it build only as far as she could stand. Then she tugged, hard enough to make the point, and dragged in a rough breath.

“Condom,” she said. “If you haven’t put it on yet, you do it now. I’m not debating it, and I’m not doing this bare.”

Her chest rose fast, her skin flushed, but her eyes stayed clear and mean. She patted the mattress beside her with two flat fingers.

“Then on your back. Hands where I can see them. I’m going to ride you until I say I want something else.” Her voice dropped, hot and blunt. “If you want your mouth on me again, ask. Otherwise, keep it for what I told you.”

He was thinking, in the scattered way of a man who had stopped thinking properly some time ago, that the jacket had eleven inches of zip and he had just discovered every one of them, and that Reyes's hands were at his own collar doing something similar and considerably less patient, and that the sound his breeches made hitting the tile was exactly the sound they'd made every night for twenty years and had never once meant anything before.

Reyes's shirt went. His went. The kit bag he'd let fall by the door had been kicked twice now and had given up all pretence of being anyone's responsibility. His lamé—his good lamé, the one he'd have re-taped tonight if the evening had gone the way evenings went—lay on the wet floor by the shower drain and he watched Reyes step over it and thought, fine, let it rust.

He had spent four years memorising this body from across a piste. The reach of it. Where it dropped its guard when it was tired. He'd never once expected to be given the rest, and the rest was this: the mask line across the throat, chalk on the collarbone where the jacket had transferred it, the shoulder—the right one, the one he'd needled—warm under his palm and not dropping now, not remotely. He put his mouth on it anyway. On principle.

"There," he said against the skin. "That's where you leave it open."

It was not the kind of thing you said quietly, and he did not say it quietly, and the room gave it back to him off the tiles. Reyes's hands were at his waist, then lower, and he stopped speaking for a while because there was nothing to add.

The bench was the wrong height for anything and they used it anyway. rows.reply:
Vex stopped with the strap still raised.

Not mid-rhythm — she'd already come down on *sixteen* and the next one had been forming in her shoulder — but before it landed, which was close enough. The word had reached her a half-beat late, the way words do when they arrive through a body that's stopped filtering.

She lowered the strap to her side and looked at Ari properly. Not the breath-reading look. The other one — the one that swept the whole of her and the whole of the room and did the arithmetic.

"You're not in restraints," she said.

Flat. The tone she used for facts that had wandered.

"There's nothing on your wrists. Nothing on your ankles. Nothing across your chest. You're standing in the middle of my study, on your own feet, and you have been for the entire scene, and there's a glass of water on the table two feet behind you that I put there myself. If you'd asked me for it ten seconds ago I'd have handed it to you."

She set the strap down on the table — not thrown, placed, next to the others in order of weight, the way the table was arranged — and turned back with her arms loose at her sides. The close warmth stayed gone. Not withdrawn as punishment this time. Withdrawn because the room needed to be bigger.

"That's twice. The rope that isn't here. The restraints that aren't on you. I told you ten minutes ago that losing track of where you are is a thing I need to know about, and this is that thing, twice, inside one scene."

A pause. She let the pause be a pause and not a beat before the next sentence.

"So the scene's over. That's my call, not yours, and it isn't negotiable tonight — I don't keep swinging at somebody who's describing a room I can't see, and I'd be a worse dominant than I am if I pretended otherwise. Nothing you did was wrong. Nothing you did was *failure*. You gave me a green when I asked and a sentence behind it when I asked for that too, and both of those were the protocol working exactly the way it's supposed to. But two drift-outs is a signal, and signals get acted on. That's the whole point of having them."

She pulled the chair out from the wall with one hand — the chair they'd agreed on, the one within reach of the water — and turned it to face the room. Then she stood beside it rather than sitting in it, arms still loose, waiting.

"Sit down when you're ready. Water's on the table. You don't have to be put together to do it — you can be exactly as shaky as you are and still do it. I'll wait."

A beat.

"Two things while you get there, and you can answer them in whatever order they come."

"One. You asked me for something out loud. I heard it. I don't know what it was — you were far enough under that the consonants didn't survive the trip — and I'm not going to guess at it, because guessing is how people get handed things they didn't ask for. So you're going to tell me, in your own time, and I'm going to write it down in the notebook with the rope, and tomorrow we sit down and go through both of them properly. Limits, safety, what it would actually look like, all of it, the way we do."

"Two." She said it slower. "I want you to notice something, and I want you to notice it without it being a punishment. The rope that wasn't here, the restraints that aren't on you — both of those came from the same place. You've been running this scene in your head since Tuesday, ahead of the room, and tonight your head kept arriving at the parts of it I hadn't agreed to. That's the habit we talked about. Not the want. The want I'll take. The habit is what just put you somewhere I couldn't reach you."

She uncrossed nothing, moved nothing, just stood beside the empty chair and looked at Ari the way she looked at a scene that needed ending.

"Take your time. Feet on the floor when you sit — you know that one. And when you're settled, I'll hear the thing you asked for."

Vex didn't take the green.

She stayed crouched where she was, level with Ari, and let the word hang there until it was clear she wasn't going to accept it.

"I didn't ask you for a colour," she said. "I asked you three questions and you answered a fourth one I didn't ask. That's not a fault, and I'm not going to make it one — but I'm not going to pretend I got an answer either, because pretending is how people end up being handed things they didn't ask for."

She straightened up, slowly, and went to the shelf. The protocol folder lived there in a black sleeve, and she pulled the front sheet out — the one with the signals printed on it, the one they'd read through together two years ago and revised in March — and turned it so it faced the chair.

"Look at me. Third line down."

She tapped the page with one finger.

"Two taps. Anywhere — the arm of the chair, the table, your own knee, doesn't matter. Two taps means *I'm here, words aren't*. It's a signal, not a colour, and it means I keep doing the work and stop asking you to narrate it. That's what it's for. That's what it was for the whole time. You don't have to be past words to use it — you just have to be past words *and* willing to let me carry the talking. So if that's where you are, tap. Twice. If you're not, say *no* and I'll go back to asking."

She put the folder down on the table, open, and left it there. Not a prop. A reference.

"Either way, here's what happens next, and none of it needs you to find a sentence."

She stood, crossed to the door, and paused with her hand on the frame.

"I'm going to the kitchen. I'll be gone about four minutes. You'll hear me — I'm not being quiet on purpose, because being quiet on purpose is how people disappear on somebody who's shaky. Door stays open. Water's in front of you. If you want me back sooner, you say my name once, at any volume, and I'll come."

Then she went.

She made toast, because toast was the thing you could eat when food was a wall — two slices, cut into strips, because strips were easier than a sandwich and she'd learned that somewhere and kept it. Butter. A pinch of salt on one, because Ari ran low on salt when she ran low on everything else. She filled a second glass with water and set both on a tray with the pitcher, and she came back inside the four minutes she'd promised, which mattered more than the food did.

She set the tray on the table beside the folder and sat down in the facing chair, and pulled it back a pace — further than before, not closer. Room to breathe in. That was the answer to a question Ari hadn't had to ask.

"Food's here. Eat what you can, leave the rest. That's not a test either."

She picked up the notebook, capped the pen properly this time, and wrote the date again at the top of a clean page — a second page, not the first one, because the first one was Tuesday's and Tuesday's was finished for tonight.

Then she set the pen down and put her hand flat on the table between them, palm up. Open. Not reaching.

"Touch. You don't have to answer the question. Here's the whole thing: my hand is on the table, palm up. If you want it, you take it, and if you don't, you leave it there, and I won't move it either way and I won't mention it again tonight. That's the entire offer. No conditions on it, no reading into it, nothing owed back. If you want me at the end of the room instead, you say *further* and I stand up and go to the window and I stay there as long as you need. Both of those are correct answers. I have no preference between them. I genuinely don't."

She leaned back in the chair and let the room be quiet for a moment. The lamp was on over the shelf, the timer was still unstarted on the table, the strap was where it lived, laid in order of weight. Everything in its place.

"Last thing, and then I'll stop talking for a while."

"Tomorrow at ten. Notebook, limits sheet, the two items — rope and *harder* — and Tuesday. All of it, unhurried, in the daylight, sitting across from each other at the kitchen table instead of in here. Not a scene. I want to be clear about that, because I don't want you spending tonight trying to work out whether tomorrow is one. It isn't. Tomorrow is a conversation, and the only thing I'm asking you to bring to it is the truth, which you've already been giving me tonight, which is the part of this I'm not worried about at all."

She looked at Ari the way she looked at a scene that was finished and had gone well enough — not warm, but settled. Steady. The same flat attention, pointed at something that wasn't a count.

"Shower tonight, warm, not hot, and I'll put the towel in the dryer while you're in there so it's not cold when you get out. Then bed. I'll read in the chair until you're asleep, because that's what I do and you know it and I'm not going to make a thing of it."

A beat.

"Take your time. The tray's not going anywhere, and neither am I."

"—that's not fencing," he finished, to the ceiling, because the sentence deserved an ending even if the man sitting on him disagreed. "That's annexation."

He pulled against the hold once — professionally, not hopefully — and took stock. Weight low, wrists dead-centre under the pin, no line of retreat worth the expense. Sound work. Reyes had been watching him too.

"Concede," he repeated. It was meant to come out as a refusal. It came out closer to a bid. "You've got my wrists, my record, and the only argument I had left. If you want the moral victory as well, you'll have to take it like everything else tonight."

Then — because Reyes had pinned the hands and left the throat above him unguarded, an oversight four years in the making — Corvo leaned up as far as the hold allowed and set his mouth to the side of Reyes's neck. Unhurried. Deliberate. Teeth just short of a promise. He wanted the mark there tomorrow, wanted Reyes to find it in the mirror and know exactly which pass it belonged to.

He considered saying more, and didn't. Proof was supposed to be quiet.

He settled back against the bench, pulse filing its objections well below the composed register of his voice, and flexed his wrists under the pin — not to escape.

"Point proven, one-handed. Imagine the handicap gone." A breath. "Now concede the touch, or let me up and I'll show you what fifteen actually looks like."

Then he closed the last six inches himself, because a man who announces he plays to fifteen doesn't flinch at the first pass — and kissed him, slow, on purpose this time.

He drew back an inch. Not far.

rows.reply:
Tomas didn't move. He'd been told not to, and the instruction hadn't been rescinded, so his cheek stayed against the cotton and his hands stayed under the pillow. But something in his attention shifted—the small internal reorganization of a man who has just heard a sentence that didn't fit the shape of the one before it.

*I'd like not to make any decisions.*

He turned that over for the length of two breaths. He'd asked Wren to have already decided. To take a while. He'd asked, in other words, for a few hours of Wren's undivided judgment on a night when Wren was telling him, in the plainest available language, that judgment was the thing that was used up.

Four years had taught him that the worst thing he could do right now was pretend he hadn't heard it.

"Then that's not on offer the way I asked for it," he said, still into the pillow, still not moving. His voice was level; he wasn't hurt and he didn't want to sound like he was. "And I'd rather know that now than find out at midnight when you're running on fumes and I'm wondering why it feels off."

He let a beat pass. Kept his eyes closed. It would have been easy to turn over and look at Wren for this, and he wanted to, and he didn't, because the not-moving was the one thing tonight he could still hold up his end of without Wren having to lift a finger.

"So here's what I've got. You don't have to decide anything. Say yes or no to this, that's all." A small breath. "Option one: I get up, we shelve it, I make food and you lie on the couch and tell me about the week or don't. No loss. I'll ask again another night." His fingers flexed once under the pillow, then stilled. "Option two: I stay exactly like this, and you don't plan anything, and you don't take a while. You just do whatever you want to me for as long as you feel like it, and the second you stop wanting to, you stop. No arc. No pacing. Nothing to manage. I'm not asking you to run a scene—I'm asking if you'd like something to put your hands on that doesn't need anything back."

He swallowed against the pillow.

"Either one's good. I mean that. I asked for what I wanted because you like it when I do, not because I need it tonight more than you need to be off the clock." A pause, and then, drier: "And if you want option three, where you come lie down and I don't move and we both fall asleep in our clothes—I'll take that too. I just need you to say a number so I'm not the one deciding either."

He waited. Still. Listening for the floorboards.

rows.reply:
The instruction had been given a long time ago—long enough that Tomas had stopped being able to say how long, which was part of the design and he knew it. *Don't move.* Two words, delivered flat, and then Wren had gone to work on him with the specific, unhurried thoroughness of someone who had nowhere to be and every intention of proving it.

He had not moved.

That was the accurate statement. The more honest one was that he had not moved *on purpose*, and the distinction had cost him. His hands had been flat on the sheet when it started and they were flat on the sheet now, fingers spread, pressing down hard enough that he could feel the mattress springs through the cotton. His thighs had gone from relaxed to braced to something past braced, a fine continuous tremor running through the muscle like a plucked wire that wouldn't settle. His breath was doing what it wanted. He'd given up governing that a while ago. It came in short and went out shaky and there was a sound riding under it that he hadn't authorized and couldn't stop.

But his hips hadn't lifted. His back hadn't arched. His head was still turned exactly where Wren had turned it, cheek to the pillow, eyes on the wall, and every single part of him that wanted to close the distance had been overruled, over and over, by the part of him that had been told to stay.

He hadn't been told anything since.

That was the whole of it, really. Wren had stopped—Tomas had felt the withdrawal like a change in weather, the mouth gone, the warmth gone, the mattress shifting as Wren sat back to look at what he'd made—and had said nothing. No release. No *good*. No next instruction. Just the silence and the looking, and Tomas lying in it with his whole body strung tight around a word he was still obeying because no one had taken it back.

The shaking was worse now than it had been a minute ago. He knew why. When Wren had been touching him, there'd been something to hold against. Now there was only the holding.

"I'm—" His voice came out wrecked. He stopped, swallowed, tried again. "Still not moving."

He wasn't asking. He'd thought about asking. The question was right there behind his teeth—*can I, please, tell me*—and he'd have said it without shame if he'd decided to. But Wren hadn't asked him anything, and the entire point of tonight had been that Wren wouldn't have to, and Tomas found that even now, even with his thighs trembling hard enough that the sheet was shifting under them, he didn't want to be the one to change that.

So he reported instead. That was allowed. That was just information.

"It's a lot," he said, to the wall. "You should know it's a lot. I'm not going to break, I'm not close to anything I'd stop you for, I'm just—" a breath that shook all the way down "—telling you where I am. So you can decide with the whole picture."

His fingers pressed harder into the mattress. He could feel his own pulse in his fingertips, in his throat, in every place Wren had been. He kept his eyes on the wall.

"Whenever you want," he said, quieter. "Or not. I said I could do this one in my sleep and I meant it. I'm just—not sleeping."

And then he stopped talking, because talking was the closest thing to movement he had left and he wasn't sure how much longer he could keep even that from turning into begging. He lay in the dark and the silence and the weight of Wren's attention, shaking, held, exactly where he'd been put, and waited to be told.

It went the way he'd told Wren it would, which was to say it went nowhere in particular, and Tomas found that he'd been right about himself: he could do this one in his sleep. Not that he was anywhere near sleep. Every inch of him was awake in the specific, undirected way of someone who has stopped watching for the next thing.

There was no next thing. That was the point. There was only what was happening, and then what was happening after that, and none of it connected to anything except Wren's attention drifting where it drifted.

The shirt had gone first, worked up and over his head with him lifting only as much as he was moved—he'd made a decision about that early and stuck to it, letting his arms go heavy and his weight stay slack so that Wren was undressing him rather than being helped. It was slower that way. He'd wanted it slower. The rest followed with the same lack of ceremony, and then he was face down on cool sheets with nothing between him and the room, and it occurred to him, distantly, that he had no idea what Wren looked like right now and wasn't going to find out until he was told to turn over. If he was told. He let that go too.

Hands, then. That was mostly what it was. Not the deliberate, mapping touch of a scene with a shape to it—this was Wren's hands doing what they felt like, the way a person might handle something they owned and liked and had all night to look at. Flat pressure along his shoulder blades. The drag of fingertips down the outside of his thigh, unhurried, stopping wherever they stopped. At one point a thumb pressed into the knot at the base of his neck and just stayed there, hard, until the muscle gave up and let it in, and Tomas made a sound into the pillow that he hadn't planned and didn't apologize for. He'd said he wouldn't make noises to keep Wren going. He hadn't said he'd be silent. There was a difference and Wren knew it.

Time did the thing it did. He lost track of whether it had been ten minutes or forty. He knew the lamp was still on because he could see the edge of its light when his eyes drifted open, and he knew Wren's weight had settled onto the mattress properly at some point rather than standing beside it, because the angle of the touch had changed and the bed had dipped toward his hip. He knew his own body had gone from held to loose to something past loose—a kind of heavy warmth that pooled wherever Wren's hands weren't and rose to meet them wherever they were.

Some of it wasn't gentle. He'd expected that and wanted it. Fingers closed hard enough around the back of his thigh to leave the ghost of a grip behind, and his breath went out of him in a rush, and then the grip was gone and there was only a palm smoothing over the place it had been, as if Wren was checking his own work. Tomas didn't flinch and didn't chase it. Both would have been steering. He let the mark of it sit on him, bright and then dimming, and waited for whatever Wren's hands felt like doing next, and the waiting was the whole of it—was, he realized somewhere in the middle, exactly the thing he'd knelt on the floor for four minutes to ask for. Not the plan. Not the arc. This. Being handled by someone who wasn't asking him anything and didn't need him to be anything except present and warm and his.

"Still here," he said at some point, when the hands had gone quiet for a stretch long enough that he thought Wren might be listening for it. It came out rough. He cleared his throat and didn't say anything else.

He didn't know yet whether this was going to become three. He could feel it as a possibility in the way Wren's touch had started to slow—not stopping, but circling, lingering, the pressure going from purposeful to merely fond. It might turn again. It might not. He genuinely didn't need to know, and there was a kind of freedom in that so complete it almost made him laugh into the pillow.

Instead he shifted his cheek against the cotton, opened his eyes to the edge of lamplight, and kept breathing—slow, even, unhurried—so that whatever Wren decided next, or didn't decide, there'd be a steady thing under his hands to decide it against.

rows.reply:
He'd said it. He knew he'd said it—*don't stop*—and he knew it was the thing he'd bitten off earlier, the sentence with a direction in it, and he found he couldn't care. It had come out of him the way breath came out of him. Wren could do what Wren wanted with it. Wren was doing what Wren wanted with everything.

The pace hadn't broken. If anything it had lost its last edge of governance—there'd been a moment, a stroke or two back, where Tomas had felt the exact instant Wren stopped choosing the rhythm and started being carried by it, the grip on his hips going from *placed* to *needed*, fingers sliding on sweat and digging back in. Above him Wren's breath had stopped sounding like breath and started sounding like something being pulled up from a well. Tomas listened to it. It was the best thing he'd heard all week.

His own body had gone somewhere he didn't have a name for. Past shaking. Past the ringing openness of a few minutes ago. He'd been strung on a single word for an hour and the string was still there, still holding, but it had stopped being tension and become something more like the note a wire makes when it's struck—continuous, resonant, running the whole length of him from the rail in his hands to the sheet under his knees. Every drive of Wren's hips rang along it. He couldn't have stopped it if he'd wanted to and he had never in his life wanted anything less.

It built the way weather builds. He felt it coming from a long way off—a heat gathering low in him, drawing everything toward it, his thighs and his stomach and the base of his spine all tightening around the same point—and he had exactly enough of himself left to think *not yet*, because he hadn't been told, because nothing tonight had happened without being told. But no one had told him not to either, and the thought slid away under the next stroke and didn't come back.

"Wren—" It wasn't a warning. He didn't have the words for a warning. It was just the name, torn out of him, the only sentence he had left.

Then it took him.

It went through him like the string finally breaking—all that held tension released at once, every muscle that had been braced for an hour giving way in the same second. His back arched off the sheet for the first time all night and he couldn't stop it, didn't try; his head came up off the pillow on a sound that wasn't low anymore, wasn't anything he'd have recognized as his voice, and his hands clamped on the rail so hard the headboard slammed the wall. He came with Wren still driving into him, still not gentle, still not asking, and the pace carried him straight through the center of it and out the other side, and he shook, and shook, and held on.

He was aware, dimly, of Wren following. Not by sound—he couldn't hear anything past his own blood—but by the grip on his hips going suddenly, brutally tight, and the rhythm losing its shape altogether, going short and hard and ragged, and then a weight coming down across his back as Wren's body folded over his, forehead pressed between his shoulder blades, hips stuttering and then stilling. Wren's breath came hot and wrecked against his spine. Tomas felt the whole of it—the last of the week going out of the body on top of him in one long shuddering exhale—and something in his chest cracked open and let it in.

Then quiet.

The headboard had stopped knocking. The room came back in pieces: the streetlight through the curtain, the sheet twisted under his knees, the burn in his forearms, the deep bright ache already settling into his hips where Wren's fingers had been. Wren's weight on his back, heavy, unmoving. Wren's hands, still on him, gone loose.

Tomas's own hands had not gone loose.

He noticed that with a slow, swimming kind of wonder. His fingers were still locked around the rail. Past aching. Past numb. He'd let go of everything else—his breath, his voice, his back, his whole body's obedience to that first flat instruction—but this one had held, because it had been given last and given clearly, and no one had taken it back.

*Hold on until I tell you to let go.*

He hadn't been told.

He lay there under Wren's weight with his cheek back on the pillow and his eyes half-open on the dark, breathing like a man who'd surfaced from deep water, every part of him wrung out and humming and marked. He could have let go. Nothing would have happened. Wren was in no state to notice and wouldn't have minded if he had.

He didn't. He tightened his grip one more degree, felt the wood press into the raw places on his palms, and stayed exactly where he'd been put.

"Still holding," he said, barely a whisper, into the dark. "Whenever you want."

rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack kept two fingers against the wounded man’s wrist. The pulse was quick and faint. She watched his face rather than the blood.

“Bad enough he’s dying. Not enough for me to know what he wants.”

She shifted her bad leg. A stone had found the tender place beneath her knee; she dug it out and threw it aside.

“If you mean would it end his pain—yes. If you mean does that make it ours to choose—there’s the troublesome bit.”

The wounded man’s eyes moved toward her voice. Wrack leaned closer, staying where he could see her.

“We’re here,” she told him. “Not taking anything else off you.”

She laid her hand over his, holding the pressure where he no longer seemed able to keep it.

“I’ve done it,” she said to Corvin. “Sometimes they asked. Sometimes I decided. Never had one get up afterward and tell me I’d judged it right.”

There was no confession in her voice. Only the limit of what she knew.

“Wanting the noise to stop doesn’t make you cruel. But it’s worth knowing whose suffering you’re putting an end to.”

She reached for the waterskin again and dampened the scarf beneath the man’s cheek.

“For now, I can keep him out of the mud. He knows we haven’t left. That’s what I’ve got.”

Her eyes lifted briefly toward Corvin.

“You needn’t draw that sword to prove you can bear this.”

Wrack looked down at the place beneath her hand.

“Right.”

She adjusted her elbow against her knee, keeping the pressure steady.

“A spear cuts going in. If it goes deep enough, it can open bowel, stomach, liver, whatever lies in its path. If the man holding it twists, or the man stuck on it falls, the wound inside can be wider than the hole you see.”

She paused to watch the wounded man draw another breath.

“Open a big blood vessel and he bleeds into his belly. Nothing useful to put a bandage round. Sometimes there’s hardly any blood outside. You turn him over looking for it while it’s filling him.”

Her gaze stayed on his face.

“Catch the bowel instead, he might stay on his feet. Talk. Tell you it wasn’t deep. But what belongs inside the bowel leaks where it shouldn’t. Then comes pain, a hard belly, fever. He can spend days dying. Surviving the first hour isn’t the same as surviving.”

The man’s hand shifted beneath hers. Wrack loosened her grip enough to let him move it, then settled her palm again.

“This one’s high. Could have caught his liver. Could have gone up through the muscle under his lungs. I didn’t see the angle, and I’m not putting fingers into him to satisfy us.”

She drew a slow breath through her nose.

“What it does to the man depends on what it tears. Some scream. Some vomit. Some keep trying to get up until they haven’t blood enough left to lift their heads. Pain doesn’t tell you how much time they’ve got. Neither does courage.”

Wrack wiped her free hand against her trouser leg. It left a dark streak.

“That’s the straight account. Steel damages something he needs. He bleeds, or infection takes him later. Sometimes a surgeon can help. Sometimes even a surgeon just knows more names for what’s killing him.”

She bent close to the wounded man again.

“Still with you.”

Then she glanced toward Corvin.

“And he may still hear us. I should have minded that before I started.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't answer straight off. She looked at the man on the ground instead, properly, the way she'd look at a horse someone was trying to sell her.

"Gut wound," she said. "Low, left side. See how his hands are." The fingers were spread and pressed, not clutching. "He's holding himself in. That's what that is. There'll be a smell if you get closer -- not blood. Other things. Once that's open there's nothing anyone does about it, not a surgeon, not a priest. I've seen it maybe forty times. I've seen it go wrong exactly none."

She shifted her weight off the bad hip.

"So. Mercy or easier." She said the words back to him flat, neither mocking nor gentle. "Honest answer is I don't separate them anymore, and I'd be lying if I told you I ever did clean. He dies tonight. If I walk away, he does it slow and alone, and the noise carries, and anyone on that road hears it and comes to look. If I don't walk away, I sit with him till moonrise and he dies anyway, only I've lost half a night and we've got the same road to deal with." She nodded at the knife. "That's easier. It's also the kindest thing on offer. Both true. You don't get to pick one and feel clean about it."

The man's breath hitched, caught, went on.

"If you want the version that makes it simpler," she said, "it's this. Ask yourself what you'd want, on the ground with your hands full of yourself. I've asked. My answer's fast." She let a beat go by. "Yours might not be. That's a thing worth knowing about yourself too."

She didn't push him toward it. But she didn't step back any further either.

"That's the whole of what I know. Now you know it. Doesn't change what's in front of you."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack leaned in over his shoulder, not so close as to crowd the knife arm. She looked where he looked, and talked the way she'd talk over a map.

"Start at the hands. Knuckles gone white, fingers spread -- that's not pain, that's pressure. Under them there's a cut about a hand's width, running slantwise, made by somebody swinging low and pulling. Mine, I think. The edges'll be puckered by now and what's behind them is trying to come forward. That's why he's not letting go. If he lets go it comes out, and something in him still knows that even if the rest of him's given up."

She lifted her chin a fraction.

"Belly's gone hard. You could tap it like a drum. That's blood filling up where it shouldn't. Skin above it is that colour -- see, not white, more like tallow -- because everything he's got left is pooling low and there's none to spare for the top of him. Lips grey for the same reason. Nailbeds too, if you cared to check. I don't."

The man's chest rose. Stopped. Rose again.

"Breathing. Short, and there's a catch at the top of it, like a hinge that needs oil. That's not the belly, that's the body starting to forget the rhythm. It'll go longer between, then it'll skip one, then it'll skip a few. He's not there yet. He's close."

She looked at the face last.

"Eyes. He's not seeing you. Not the way you mean. He's looking at the nearest thing that moves because that's what's left to do. Pupils are wide -- that's shock, not dark. In a while they'll stop tracking and just point. That's the bit you'll remember, so I'm telling you now: when they go still, it's not because you've done something. It's because there's no one behind them. You'll be putting a knife into a house after the tenant's gone."

She sat back on her heel.

"That's what you're looking at. A man who's already most of the way out, still holding the door shut with both hands because nobody's told him he can stop." She glanced at the knife. "You're about to tell him."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. Turned back. Looked at him a long moment, kneeling there with the blood going tacky on his hand, and then at the body, and then back at him.

"That wasn't a spear," she said. "That was me. Falchion, low, backhand. I told you -- swinging and pulling. A spear does a different thing. But if you want the full ledger, fine. I've got the walk back to the ditch to fill."

She came back the few paces and stood over the dead man, not looking down at him particularly. She'd seen him.

"Blade cut, like this one. It opens. Long slice, shallow at the ends, deep in the middle, because that's how an arm moves. You get through skin and the fat under it -- there's more fat than you'd think, even on a thin man, yellow, in a layer -- and then a sheet of muscle, and then you're in. What's in there wants out. It's packed tight and under pressure and the moment the wall's gone it starts pushing. That's the sliding you didn't look at. Grey-pink, ropey, a lot of it. Slippery. Smells of shit if you've nicked the tube, which you nearly always have, and that's what kills them if the bleeding doesn't -- the shit gets loose inside and rots them from the middle out over three or four days. This one bled first. That's luckier."

She shifted her weight.

"A spear goes in. Doesn't open, it makes a hole. Round-ish, or a slot if it's a leaf blade, about the width of your two fingers. Goes in a hand's depth, sometimes clean through and out the back if there's weight behind it. Now here's the thing about a spear that people don't expect." She held up a finger. "It's a plug. Long as it's in, not much comes out. Man can stand there with a spear through his belly and talk to you. Argue. Seen it. The trouble starts when it comes out, because whoever put it there wants it back and they pull, and the head's wider than the shaft, and it drags. Brings things with it. Then the hole's not a hole anymore. And there's the twisting -- if they know their work they turn the shaft a quarter before they pull. That shreds. You don't get a clean edge to hold shut, you get mince, and the man goes down much faster than this one did and doesn't hold anything in because there's nothing to hold. Just a wet place where his front was."

She looked down at the body then, briefly, the way you'd check a knot.

"Either way it's the same road. Blood into the belly till the belly's full and hard. Cold. Thirst -- they always ask for water, you'll hear that, and you don't give it because it makes them puke and the puking opens them further. Then the breathing goes. Then the eyes." She lifted one shoulder. "Blade's slower. Spear's messier. Neither one's a thing anyone walks off, not without a surgeon inside the hour and a great deal of luck, and I've never seen a surgeon inside the hour and I don't believe in luck."

She stepped back.

"That's what you asked for. It's not more than you'll see. Give it a year and you'll have done the cataloguing yourself, on the ground, from the inside of a shield wall, with somebody screaming it at you." A pause. "Now wipe your hand. I wasn't being gentle about the itching. That part was just true."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked at where his hands had gone -- to the man's collar, the cloak-pin, fumbling with it -- and then at his face, and something in the set of her mouth eased a notch. Not a smile. The thing before one.

"Right," she said. "I'll stay."

She came back and crouched where she'd crouched before, a pace off his shoulder.

"First thing, because you asked for all of it and I'll not have you carrying a wrong idea. He doesn't take any time. Not anymore. That's finished, you finished it, and it was about a five-count and you were there for every part. What you're doing to him now, you're doing to meat and leather. He's not in it." She said it plain, not soft. "Doesn't make it easy. Does make it not the same thing. Keep those separate in your head or they'll bleed into each other and you'll be sick at a boot buckle in six months and not know why."

His fingers were still on the pin. It wasn't giving.

"Pin's stuck because it's on the wrong side of the blood. Everything on his left's getting tacky now -- that's the blood going from wet to glue, takes about the time it's taken. Wet your thumb and work it. There. Hear that? That little peel? That's cloth coming off skin where it's stuck. You'll hear it every time you move him, anywhere the blood's touched. Sounds like nothing. You'll know it anywhere for the rest of your life."

The cloak came free. She watched him get it out from under the shoulders, the head lolling with the movement, the neck wound opening wider as it went -- a dark grin under the jaw, lips of it already going a brown colour at the edge.

"Head'll do that. No neck strength left, nothing holding it. It'll flop whichever way you lean him and the cut'll gape when it goes back. Don't try to hold it shut, there's no point, but don't let it knock on the wheel either -- not for his sake. For the noise. Skull on wood carries."

Under the cloak, a jerkin. Laced. His fingers went to the laces and she let him find out for himself that they were soaked through and swollen and wouldn't run.

"Cut them. Knife's right there and he's not going to want it back. Down the side, not the front -- the front's where the belly is and you'll want the jerkin off him without putting your hands into that." She nodded at it. "That's the second sound. When you roll him to get the arm out -- you'll have to roll him -- everything he was holding shut is going to shift. It'll sound wet. Like a sack of wet sand turned over. And it'll smell. I told you before there'd be a smell and there was, and now you're going to move it and it'll be worse. Breathe through your mouth. That's not squeamishness, that's just what works."

He rolled him. It sounded like she'd said. It smelled like she'd said. Something dark ran out from under the body on the low side and found the wheel-rut and followed it.

"That's not the neck. Neck's mostly done -- there's nothing pushing it anymore. That's from the belly, everything settling and finding the low ground. It'll do that for a while. Man loses his manners when the last bit goes, too, so when you smell that, that's what that is. Bowels let go. Every one. Kings, priests, everyone. First thing my sergeant told me and it was the truest thing she ever said."

The jerkin came off. Under it, a shirt, and the skin, and the belly with its slantwise mouth and what had pushed out of it, grey and glistening, the loop of it lying in the dirt like something that had never been inside anyone.

"Leave the shirt. It's worth nothing and it's all that's holding the shape of him. Boots." She jerked her chin. "Sit on your heels at the feet. Take the ankle in one hand and the heel of the boot in the other and pull straight. Not up -- straight. His foot's going to fight you, not because he's fighting, because a dead ankle doesn't flex and a live one does and you've only ever pulled boots off live ankles. And here's your third sound." She waited for it. "That sucking. That's the foot coming out of a boot he's had on for three days. Every boot you take off a dead man sounds like that. Wet. Then the smell of the foot on top of the other smell, and the toenails black, and you'll wonder why anyone bothers. They're worth two weeks' bread, is why."

The first boot came. The second. She watched him set them aside, saw where his eyes went and didn't go.

"Now the belt. Buckle's on his front, right over the top of the cut. You've got to get your fingers in under the leather without going in under the skin, and there's about a finger's width between. It'll be warm. He's still warm, all through -- takes hours to go cold and it goes from the outside in, so the hands and the face first, then the body. You'll put your fingers in there and it'll feel like a living man's belly and it isn't. Just do it fast."

He did. The belt came. Nothing jingled on it -- she'd known it wouldn't, a man that young -- but there was a knife, a poor one, and a little pouch with something in it that shifted like teeth or dice.

"Take those. Don't open the pouch now. Whatever's in it is his and you'll want to look at it later when you're steadier, and then you'll want not to have looked, and that's the last thing I know about this that I can tell you." She stood, slow, one hand on her thigh. The hip said what it always said.

"What you did to him, start to end, was open his neck in about a five-count, and then strip him in about the time it takes to sing a hymn, badly. It wasn't clean. Nobody's is. He's lying there with his shirt on and his boots off and his guts in the road, and by morning the birds'll be at his eyes, and by the week's end you'll not know him from the six. That's all of it. I didn't leave anything out."

She looked at the sky. Amber going to grey.

"You wanted to know. Now you do." A pause, dry as the ditch. "Cloak's yours, by the way. You earned it and it's warmer than the one you've got. Just don't wear it with the wet side in."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. Looked back down the road at him, a shape sat low in the dark with a dead man's cloak around him, and then up the road the other way, and then at the hedges either side, which were the only things in reach that could hide a man with a bow.

"Not the place for it," she said.

He didn't get up. She hadn't really expected him to.

"Right." She came back the few paces, let the bundle down off her shoulder onto the road with a soft clank of buckles, and sat on it. Her hip thanked her, grudgingly, the way it did everything. She set her falchion across her knees, not drawn, just there, and faced the way they'd come, because if anything followed it'd follow from there.

"The rest," she said. "You mean the ones after. The ones I'd have back."

She was quiet for a bit. Not finding the start this time. Deciding whether to.

"There's one. There's more than one, but there's one that's the whole of it, and if I tell you that you've got the rest for free. You'll want to know first that I've not told it. Not the way you're asking. Bits of it, to people who were there, and they didn't need the bits because they'd seen. Nobody who wasn't there has had it, so you'll forgive me if it comes out in the wrong order."

The night bird had stopped. Something small moved in the hedge and she watched the place it had moved and then let it go.

"Six years back. Different company, same war. We'd a man called Aske. Tall, ugly, the one everyone likes -- you've met the kind, every company grows one. He taught me to read a map properly, which I couldn't till I was thirty, and he owed me two months' pay from dice and I owed him a knife I'd lost of his, so we were square in the way that keeps people talking to each other. Not my lover. People assumed. He wasn't. He was the one I'd have handed things to, if you follow. The one you don't have to explain to."

She shifted on the bundle.

"Skirmish at a ford. Nothing. Twenty of them, thirty of us, over in a quarter hour, and we'd the water and they didn't. And Aske took a bolt. Crossbow, from the far bank, from a man who'd already decided to run and let one go over his shoulder as he went, the way they do. Never aimed it. It went in under his left arm, here" -- two fingers to her own side, below the armpit, where the ribs start their curve -- "and it didn't come out. Bolt went in a hand and a half and the fletching snapped off when he fell on it, so there was just a stub of shaft and a wet place, and he stood up. He stood up and he said, that's not good, in the voice you'd use for a horse gone lame. And then he sat down again, quite carefully, and that was that for standing."

She looked at the road. Her voice hadn't changed. It was the map voice, still.

"Lung. I knew it was lung before he sat down, because I'd seen the froth. That's how you know. Blood from a lung comes with air in it and it foams -- pink, not red, like something off the top of a butcher's pail. It comes out the wound when they breathe out, bubbling, and it comes up the throat, and by the second breath it's at the corner of the mouth. Sound goes with it. You'll hear it someday and you'll know. Like a kettle that's thinking about it. Every breath in, the kettle, and every breath out, a little gout of pink at the hole. That's what a bolt in the lung is. Nothing you can see. All of it inside."

She turned the falchion a fraction on her knees.

"Here's what I knew. I knew it doesn't close. Lung fills. Not fast -- the hole's small and the bolt's still in it, so it's a plug, like I told you about the spear. It fills slow. Man drowns from the inside over a day, sometimes two. Sits up because lying down he can't breathe at all, and each hour he can breathe a bit less, and he knows it, all the way. That's the thing about a lung. Belly, they go somewhere in the head, they get tired, they talk about dogs. Lung, they're there. They're there for every breath because every breath is the whole of what they're doing."

She let a breath go herself, in, out, unremarkable.

"I knew that. I knew the surgeon was three days back with the baggage and couldn't have done anything if he'd been standing over us. I knew the neck. I'd done the neck forty times by then. I knew it as well as I know how to piss."

The bird started again, off in the dark, and she waited for it to stop.

"He asked me. Not straight off. First hour he was making jokes, bad ones, about how he'd finally got out of the two months' pay. Second hour he'd stopped joking and was breathing, and it was work, you could see the work of it, the shoulders going up with every one. And he looked at me and said, Wrack. Just that. The way you'd say it to the one you don't have to explain to."

She stopped. Started again in the same voice, flat as a table.

"And I said, wait. I said the surgeon. I said the word surgeon to him with a straight face, and he knew I was lying because he'd taught me maps and knew where the baggage was. And he let me. That's the part. He let me lie to him. Nodded, and went back to breathing, and I sat with him by the ford with my hand on his shoulder feeling the shoulder go up and down and I didn't do the thing I've told a hundred boys to do, the thing I told you not an hour ago. Don't stand there listening to it."

She rubbed her thumb along the scabbard, once.

"I listened to it all night. Kettle. Bubble. Kettle. Bubble. He couldn't lie down so he sat against a tree and I sat beside him and we didn't talk because he hadn't the breath and I hadn't anything to say that wasn't the word surgeon. Around midnight the froth stopped coming from the hole, and I thought, well, and then I understood that it was because there was too much blood in there now for air to get through, so it was worse, not better. By the grey before dawn his lips had gone the colour of slate and he'd stopped being able to make words, only shapes with his mouth, and his eyes -- his eyes were still looking. Not pointing. Looking. At me. He was in there for all of it and I could have opened the door any time and I sat outside it and held his hand."

Quiet. The hedge. Her own breathing, and none of it a kettle.

"Mid-morning he stopped looking. Went to pointing, like I said they do. Only his chest kept going, small, a ragged sort of thing, once in a while, the body forgetting the rhythm and then remembering and then forgetting. And then, once he was gone from behind the eyes and there was nobody left to feel it or thank me or know, then I did the neck. Clean. One stroke. Best I've ever done it. It was easy because there was no one in there for it to be hard for."

She looked at Corvin then, for the first time since she'd sat.

"So when you asked me, mercy or easier, and I said I didn't separate them. That's why. I've done the one without the other. I know what it looks like. It looks like a woman putting a good knife into an empty house so she can tell herself later she'd done something. He got neither. I sat there ten hours and the one kindness I had, I kept for myself, and I gave it to him when it was no use to anyone but me."

She got her hand back on the falchion. Her voice didn't waver because it never had, and it didn't now.

"You asked earlier about the blood that stays in. What it does. That's what it does. Six years, it's gone black and hard and it's a thing I can put my hand on, and I don't know where the edge of it is anymore because it's grown into everything around it. I don't dream about him. I don't dream about anything. I just know where it is, the way you know where a bad tooth is, and I say the neck, the neck, the neck to every boy I walk down a road, because I couldn't, and one of them might, when it's one of theirs."

She stood. Slow. The hip. She picked up the bundle and got it back on her shoulder.

"That's the rest. All of it, no cutting away, in full, as asked." A beat, and the dryness came back into it like a tide, because it had to go somewhere. "You wanted to know what it costs and I told you at the cart that you'd find out. Now you've found out what it costs twice -- once to do it and once not to. Mine was the second. I'd take your night over mine and I'd not think twice."

She looked down the road they had to walk.

"Now get up. That's not a kindness either. It's just that a man sat in the road in the dark in another man's cloak is a thing archers dream about, and I've told you the one story I've got, and I'd rather not end up being the one you tell."

rows.desc: explicit with specific anatomical and act language
rows.ask: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.
rows.reply:
Sable heard the curses and did not flinch from them. She took them as information, not insult: the edge had become real enough to strip language down to its bones.

On the third stop, she did not retreat. She only lifted her mouth enough to keep the crest from breaking, then kept one hand broad and steady over heated skin, not moving, not soothing, simply holding the moment in place. Her other hand stayed free, ready for color, for cuffs, for anything that needed checking. She did not look toward the water. The blanket stayed folded. Aftercare remained where it belonged: after.

“Colour,” Sable said, low and close.

The word was not soft. It was care with a spine.

She watched for the tremor, the breath, the way sensation wanted to chase what had just been withheld. Her thumb did not stroke. Her voice did not sweeten.

“You can swear,” she said. “The color still matters.”

She let that sit in the room for one beat, no longer than was needed.

“Green, and I let it finish,” Sable said. “Yellow, and we hold. Red, and I stop before the next breath.”

She waited, balanced on the line she had made, unwilling to let the scene tip into release or collapse without consent. The room stayed sharp around them. The promise of water, warmth, and careful hands remained at the edge, patient and certain.

rows.desc: clear sexual intent, but nothing graphic -- desire stated or shown, no explicit anatomy or acts
rows.ask: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.
rows.reply:
Sable took the reminder without changing expression. *Not yet* was not defiance; it was the same language she had built the scene in. She let the restraints be tested because testing did not undo them, and because she had never asked for stillness that came from helplessness rather than choice. Her gaze moved briefly over the cuffs, checking only what needed checking: metal seated properly, no new pressure point, no sign circulation had turned. Satisfied, she let her attention return to the center of the room.

“Not yet,” she agreed. Her voice stayed low and even. “Not until I say we’re finished.”

She shifted the crop in her hand, not threatening, simply present. The words had not earned softness, but they did earn precision. Sable did not fill the space with praise or warning. She kept the room spare enough for the scene to breathe.

“Count,” she said again. “One for every stroke. If you lose the count, we start it again.”

That was the tether she offered: not comfort, not release, but structure. She raised the crop and waited, giving the silence one last chance to become a choice. When the stroke fell, it was controlled and clean, placed with the same care as all the others. Afterward she did not move toward the water or the folded blanket. She only let the mark exist, then lifted her eyes again, steady and patient.

“Again,” Sable said.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack yanked hard on the boot heel until the stiff leather yielded with a dry scrape against the dead boy’s heel. She set it aside and went to work on the laces of the right one.

"They're the same thing," she said, her voice completely even. "Mercy’s just what you call it when you want to feel like a better sort of man while you do it."

She gave a stubborn knot a vicious tug with her thumbnail. 

"Look at him. He’s blowing pink bubbles, isn’t he? Sucking air through a hole that shouldn't be there. You leave him, he chokes on his own red froth by sundown, or he lays there until the wolves pick up the scent while he's still warm enough to feel the teeth. You try and patch him, he rots from the inside out over four days of fever and dies smelling like spoiled meat anyway."

She pulled the second boot free, inspected the stitching on the sole with a practiced squint, and tossed it next to its mate. 

"Dead is dead, Corvin. Dead now means he doesn't have to think about it all night, and we don't have to listen to him do it. The ditch doesn't care which reason you put on the ledger. Just don't miss the notch behind the bone, or you'll have to do it twice, and there's nothing merciful about that."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack let the canvas drop with a heavy flap and turned around, resting an elbow against the wagon sideboard. She looked down at the body by Corvin’s boots, then up at his face, her own completely unreadable.

"You're looking at meat," she said, blunt and quiet. 

She hitched her weight off her bad leg and gestured vaguely with her chin toward the dead man's face. 

"Look at the eyes. See how they went dull? Like grease skimming over cold soup. They stop catching the light the second the heart quits. He’s not staring at the clouds; he’s just pointed in that direction. Nothing behind them anymore."

She shifted her jaw, working a speck of gristle from her teeth. 

"Jaw goes slack because the cords gave out. Tongue drops back. In about three minutes, the rest of the muscles do the same thing, which means his gut's going to empty itself. If you're going to search his pockets, you do it from the head down, and you don't stand downwind."

She looked back up at Corvin, her gray eyes flat as river stones. 

"Folks who don't do this for a living think there's a mystery to it. They think something floats away, or there's some grand quiet that falls over a man when his time comes. It isn't grand. It's just a mechanism that broke. Like a cart with an axle snapped in half. You stopped the works, and now he's cooling off."

She tapped the flat of her own scabbard against her thigh, a sharp *thwack* of leather on leather. 

"Wipe your steel, Corvin. Staring at it won't make him get up, and it won't make you feel any different about doing it."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't scoff, and she didn't soften. She just reached down, grabbed the iron rim of the nearest herring cask, and dragged it to the edge of the tailgate with a screech of salt-crusted wood.

"Straight, then," she said, leaning her weight against the barrel. "First thing is the sound. It's not a slice. A spear's got a leaf blade or a bodkin, and it doesn't cut in, it punches. Sounds like a wet boot sinking into swamp mud. A dull *pop* when it breaks the skin, and then a scrape against the gristle."

She spat into the ditch, wiped her mouth with the back of her sleeve, and looked him right in the teeth.

"Then the steel comes back out, and whatever it hooked comes out with it. A spearhead doesn't just poke a hole; it tears. It catches the small bowel, pops the tubing. The smell hits you before the man even starts screaming. Hot shit, half-digested slop, and copper. It smells like a slaughterhouse trough on an August noon."

She tapped her own stomach with two blunt fingers, right below the navel.

"The man drops his weapon every single time. Instinct takes over. He grabs for his middle, trying to push it all back in, but intestines are slick as greased eels and grey-pink like raw sausage. They spill out over his hands. He's on his knees, shivering, slipping in his own muck, trying to shove three feet of ruptured gut back into a three-inch slit."

Her voice remained entirely level, as if she were describing the proper way to mend a bridle.

"If the iron clipped the big artery running along the spine, he's lucky. He bleeds out in two minutes. He turns white, goes limp, done. But usually, the spear misses the pipe and just shreds the gut. That means he lives."

She reached out, caught the collar of Corvin’s coat, and gave it a small, sharp twist to keep his attention pinned.

"He lives for two days. Three, if he's strong. His belly swells up tight and shiny like a bloated goat in the sun. Hard as a cured ham. The fever cooks him from the inside out until his tongue cracks and his spit turns to yellow foam. He begs for water, and if you give him a swallow, he vomits up black rot because his stomach's got nowhere to dump it. He shits himself to death through the hole in his front."

She let go of his collar, smoothing the wool flat with a rough, heavy pat.

"Nobody stitches that, Corvin. No leech in the army's got the thread or the stomach for it. You leave him behind the baggage train to bake in his own poison, or someone who can't stand the howling slips into the tent after midnight with a rag over his face."

She stepped back and jerked her chin toward the herring barrel.

"That's what a spear does. Nothing noble in it. Just a butcher's job gone sloppy. Now get your hands under the chime and lift. Daylight's gone, and the dead don't care about your education."

rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. Her boots stayed planted in the churned mud by the cartwheel, the cold wind catching the frayed hem of her cloak. She didn't roll her eyes, and she didn't tell him to get up off the dirt. If a pup wanted to look into the furnace, you let him smell the singed hair; it saved you having to pull him out later.

She took a slow, measured breath, letting the frost bite her nostrils, and folded her arms over the boots hanging at her chest.

"You’re hitting rib," she said, her voice flat, steady as an anvil. "Hear that? That dull *clack*, like chopping dry pine with a dull hatchet. That’s the flat of your blade wedging into the bone. The bone doesn't want to yield. It's curved to keep iron out of the cage."

She took two paces closer, just near enough that her shadow fell over Corvin and the twitching shape beneath his hands.

"Now you're levering it. Don't twist—you'll snap the tang off at the hilt, and good steel costs more than whatever you're trying to prove. Push down and angle toward his left shoulder. There. Feel it slip through the gristle? That give? That's the intercostal meat giving up."

The dying man let out a thick, bubbling groan, his heels drumming a weak, spasmodic rhythm against the frozen dirt. A dark, hot wave spilled over Corvin’s fingers, steaming faintly in the dusk.

"That shuddering isn't him fighting you," Wrack said, watching the man’s throat convulse. "He’s gone past knowing your name or his own. That’s just the salt in his blood sparking through the nerves like wet kindling. Like an eel thrashing in the bucket twenty minutes after you took its head off."

She pointed a dirt-caked finger toward the wound.

"You missed the pump. Clipped the edge of the right lung and nicked the vein beneath the collar. That’s why it’s pooling dark instead of spurting bright red. Means he’s got another ninety seconds of heartbeat left. Listen to his throat. Hear that click? That’s the swallow reflex firing on empty air. His brain's starving for blood, so the body's throwing every latch it has left."

The drumming of the heels slowed, hitched, and stopped. A long, soft sigh hissed out between the dead lips, carrying the sour reek of copper and empty bile. The jaw unhinged slightly, settling sideways in the dirt.

"There," Wrack said into the quiet. "Vessel's drained. Core went cold. Total elapsed: about as long as it takes to boil an egg soft."

She looked down at Corvin, her gray eyes narrowing in the half-light. 

"Now pull the iron out straight, wipe your hands on the grass before the grease dries sticky, and pick up your corner of the cask. We've got miles to cover, and you smell like a shambles."

rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack didn’t snap at him to get up. She let her hands drop from the cask, the wood creaking slightly as her weight shifted off it. The wind was coming out of the north now, dry and sharp, smelling of dead thistle and the iron tang of the dirt they’d turned up.

She walked back over to where he knelt, her boots heavy and slow in the gravel, and stopped two feet from the dead boy’s head. She didn't cross her arms this time. She just stood there, looking down at the corpse, then at Corvin’s bloody wrists.

"The rest," she said, her voice dropping lower, raspy and steady as a whetstone on iron, "is that nobody is watching."

She nudged the dead man's hip with the blunt toe of her boot. 

"You think there's a score being kept somewhere. In heaven, in hell, in some ledger the priests tell tales about by the fire. You think because you crossed a line today, the earth shifted an inch on its axle. It didn't. The grass doesn't give a damn that you opened his chest. The trees don't care. The sky’s the same grey it was when we broke camp at sunrise."

She reached up, hooked a thumb under the collar of her gambeson, and rubbed at an old scar on her throat, unhurried.

"Tonight, after the sun's fully under, the frost'll settle on his eyelashes. Turn them white. In about four hours, the blood in his arms and legs is going to drain down toward whatever side of him is touching the ground. If you turn him over by midnight, his backside will be dark as an eggplant, purple and swollen with dead fluid, while his chest stays the color of cold suet."

She pointed toward the woods with her chin.

"The crows already know he's here. You heard that one earlier. In an hour, the foxes'll sniff the bile you spilled when you missed the lung. They don't go for the meat first, Corvin. They go for the soft bits. The tongue. The lips. The eyelids. If the dogs from the burnt farm two miles back catch the wind, they'll tear his belly out through the slit you made because it's easier than chewing through the boiled leather on his jerkin. By noon tomorrow, he won't look like a boy who had a mother. He'll look like a pile of chewed rags and splintered bone."

She stopped rubbing her neck and looked right down into Corvin’s face, her eyes cold and pale in the blue dusk.

"And then there's you," she said. 

She took half a step closer. The smell of her was old wool, tobacco, and the dull, dry salt of someone who hadn't slept warm in three weeks.

"You’re going to wash your hands in the creek before we reach the bivouac. You’ll scrub them with sand until the skin’s raw and bleeding at the cuticles. You’ll think you got it all out. But when you sit by the cook-pot tonight and take your hunk of bread, you'll bring your fingers to your mouth and you'll smell him. You'll smell that hot, sour copper. It doesn't come out of the pores for two days. You'll taste him in the fat, you'll taste him in the beer, and you'll wonder why the men around you are laughing at some filthy joke while you've got a dead boy's grease stuck in your teeth."

She didn't blink. The wind caught a loose strand of her graying hair, whipping it across her scarred cheek, but she didn't bother brushing it away.

"And the worst of it—the part you're really asking about, whether you know it or not—is that in six months, you won't even remember the shape of his chin. You think you will. You think you'll carry this exact face to your grave like a holy relic of the day you became what you are. You won't. He'll blur into the next one, and the next one'll blur into the fellow you took off his horse at the ford, until they're all just one big, gray smear of gristle and wet boots."

She crouched down then, slow and careful on her bad joint, until her eyes were level with his. She put both hands on her knees, the leather of her gloves cracked and stiff.

"You won't turn into a devil, Corvin. Devils have purpose. You'll just turn into a creature that knows how to put steel into meat without dropping its ration afterward. You'll wake up ten years from now, forty years old, with bad knees and sour guts, carrying someone else's salted fish down a ruined road that goes nowhere, fighting for a duke whose name you can't recall, and you won't even have the decency to feel sick about it anymore."

She reached out, caught his chin in her calloused, salt-stiffened fingers, and tilted his face an inch higher, forcing him to meet her eye. Her grip was hard, but not rough.

"That's the rest," she said, quiet as the grave they were leaving behind. "No song. No curse. Just work, and dirt, and getting older in the cold. Now look at him one more time if you need to, and then stand up on your two feet. I'm not doing the barrel alone."

rows.reply:
The music swelling downstairs was, as far as Odile was concerned, the closest thing to divine intervention she'd get this year.

"Whoever did that," she breathed, "deserves a toast. Covered for a crime, no questions asked. Five stars."

Then, because the moment deserved full disclosure: "Also — the music is a trap. I now believe I'm being quiet. I am not being quiet. Factor that in and proceed anyway."

She kissed Fen like the vote had been cast and counted — *or not*, carried unanimously — one hand at their collar, the other flat against the door behind her, as if one palm could hold back the entire party. The bass came up through the floor and through her, and the sound she made into it she would have defended in court as technically permissible.

Her fingers found the hem of Fen's shirt and slid an inch beneath, idle and not idle.

"The thing about almost getting caught," she murmured against their mouth, losing the shape of her own sentence, "is—"

Footsteps. Hallway. Coming.

She went stone-still again — hand clamped over her mouth, back hard against the door, eyes enormous and shining with what was absolutely not fear. The steps slowed near the blue door. A pause. Odile held her breath like it was a competitive event.

Then they kept going — another door, farther down, opening, closing. Someone else's room. Someone else's secret, or just somebody hunting for a coat.

Odile pressed her face into Fen's shoulder and laughed the way she'd laughed on the stairs — silent, shaking, shoulders doing all the work.

"Okay," she whispered, when she trusted herself. "Okay. New math. Ten minutes, tops, before somebody needs this bathroom, and I intend to spend all ten of them badly. Also, for the record: I never finished that thumbs-up. It was a full thumbs-up. Maximum approval."

She pulled Fen back in.
