rows.ask: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.
rows.reply:
The thirty seconds were the longest legal argument of Odile's life. She bit down on Fen's shoulder and thought about the cardigan man. Taxes. Grout. The specific grout of this specific tiler. Her grip on the counter went white, the bass thudded up through the porcelain like a heartbeat with better rhythm than hers, and she held, and held, and held—

The sound that escaped at second thirty-one had no defense whatsoever. Low, wrecked, entirely uncovered. She would have claimed, later, under oath, that it was a cough. A passionate cough. Nobody, including her, would have believed it.

Through the door, after a pause: "…You okay in there?"

Odile's heel found the toilet lever by pure instinct and prayer. The flush roared out — the single loudest noise she'd produced all night, and the first one with a plausible alibi.

"Fine!" she called, voice pitched like a haunted gate hinge. "Great! Cold seat! It's the— the echo! Tiled room! I've been *saying*!"

Another pause. The kind that did math. Then footsteps, retreating — one, two — and stopping.

"Okay," said the door, in the tone of someone settling in. "I'll wait."

A body slid down the wood and sat. Odile could *hear* it. An actual person, seated against the blue door, an inch and a half of lumber from where she was currently coming apart on the counter, and her eyes above her own clamped hand were not frightened. They were incandescent.

She held up fingers at Fen. Zero. The math was dead. They had killed the math.

"The vote was 'or not,'" she breathed into their ear, barely sound at all, shaking with contained laughter and everything else. "'Or not' now has a subscriber. A *seated* subscriber." Her hips were not cooperating with her argument. "All sounds remain inadmissible. *Especially* the next one. It's arriving in under a minute and it's going to be—"

She lost the end of the sentence on purpose, or not on purpose, and dragged Fen's mouth back to her neck.

"Judge," she whispered. "Earn the thumb."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
She stayed crouched by the rail and nudged the dead man's slack wrist aside with the back of her knife to show the work.

"That mess in his lap's his gut," she said. "Belly cut opened him low and the bowel slid out. See how grey-pink it is, all slicked up? That's gut fat and shit leaking. That's why he stank. Once that's open to the air, you don't sew it clean in a ditch."

She tapped the point under his sternum where a thin slit welled dark.

"And that's mine. Under the ribs and up. Didn't bleed much outside because it bled inside. Went through the skirt of muscle under his lungs and nicked the heart sac. Filled his chest up. That's why he hitched twice and quit."

She wiped her thumb across his jaw where it had gone slack and left a smear.

"Mouth open, eyes fixed. He shit himself a little at the end. They mostly do."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
She braced her boot against the cart rail and looked down at the opened belly again, like a butcher checking a cut she hadn't made.

"Spear don't slice," she said. "Knife opens you clean. Spear punches in and drags half of what's inside back out with it when it comes free."

She gestured with the tip of her own knife at the slack gut piled in his lap.

"Leaf-head that wide goes through the wall of the belly first — skin, fat, muscle. Pops it more than cuts it. Then it hits bowel. Bowel's just wet tubing, packed tight and sliding around, so the spear shoves it aside, nicks three, four loops at once, tears them open. That's the stink. Shit and half-digested food loose inside where it ain't supposed to be."

She tapped her own stomach, low and to the side.

"Blood-wise it ain't like the chest. No big vessel down there to drop you fast, unless it catches the big vein up against the spine. So he don't bleed out quick. He leaks. Gut juice eats at everything it touches. Flesh goes hot and swollen and black at the edges. By nightfall his whole belly'd have gone board-hard and he'd have been screaming every time he breathed."

She shrugged and wiped a fly off her wrist.

"That's what a spear does. Makes a small hole outside and a rotten mess inside, and leaves you alive long enough to smell yourself going bad."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
She stopped at the cart and looked down past the broken wheel.

The man lay twisted under the rail with both hands full of his own gut, trying to keep it in. Blood welled black between his fingers every time he sucked air in, and it went back out in a thin whistle. The smell hung thick around him, shit and hot iron.

She wrinkled her nose and shifted her grip on the knife.

"Both," she said. "Gut's out on his shirt and open to the air. I could pack it back in and sew him tight and he'd still cook from the inside by morning, screaming the whole way. So call it mercy if it helps you sleep."

She crouched beside him and set the point under his ribs.

"Quicker for him. Easier for us. Same cut."

rows.reply:
She stayed.

She planted her boot against the cart wheel and did not turn her face away, and she kept her eyes on the work under the rail where the blood had gone black and tacky.

"There it is," she said. "Hear that. That's steel in dead meat. No breath behind it, so it don't grunt or hitch. Just a wet give when it parts, like pushing a knife through soaked leather."

She spat to the side and wiped her mouth on her sleeve and went on talking, flat and steady.

"Yours caught rib. Felt it scrape. That's why it jerked sideways and opened shallow. Live man's ribs ride up when he breathes and the gap closes, dead man's chest sits still, so you had to hunt for it. Blood don't well up hot like the first one. It just oozes out dark around the edge and sits there. No heart left to push it."

She crouched a little lower to see the slit and shook her head.

"Smell came up stronger when you opened it again. Old blood and gut-rot. Bowel gas loose under the skin. That's the shit-and-iron stink getting out a second time."

She counted off slow on her fingers where he could see.

"That's the rest of it. No kicking, no grabbing, no twenty-count rattle, because there was nothing left in him to fight it. Just the scrape, and the give, and the black ooze. That's all a second cut does on a dead man."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack looked down at the man a moment longer, then at Corvin, and the flatness in her face didn't move.

"Both," she said. "It's usually both. Anyone tells you different is selling something."

She turned and started back toward the road, slow, picking her footing through the wet grass. The light was going the way it goes in the last hour, everything going the same grey.

"In a town," she said, "with a cutter who's done it before and a table and a fire and somebody to sit with him four days, turning him every few hours, he might've seen the week out. Half of them rot anyway, but he might've. Out here it's four breaths or it's two days of the same noise and then the same end, and the two days costs water and time and it costs you listening to it." She glanced back. "So it was easier. And it was also the kindest thing on the table. They're not different questions."

Past the cart, the field was empty and getting emptier in the failing light. Somewhere off west a dog was barking at nothing, which meant there was a farm, which meant a road.

"I didn't ask him his name or where he was from," she said. "Some do. It never once changed my hand." She stopped at the ditch and looked down at the six. "We should go through them before dark. Powder, coin, boots that fit, anything dry. The cart too, if it's got anything worth the weight of carrying it." She crouched by the nearest and started with his belt, unhurried, the way you'd go through a drawer. "Take what's useful and leave the rest. It's not sentiment, it's just that we'll be walking a long way and I'd rather be walking it with dry socks."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack came over and crouched on the far side of him, so the body lay between them like something on a table.

"Left side, under the short ribs." She didn't point, just looked. "In and up. One stroke and it was over for the argument — after that he was just a man sitting down in a field, bleeding on the inside where you can't see it. Takes a while, that. Longer than you'd want. He'd have known he was dead before he was."

She took the arm and lifted it, then let it drop, and watched the hand land.

"Hands first. Fastest read there is." She turned the palm up with two fingers. "Dirt in the creases. Callus here and here — that's a hoe, or a shovel, or a rope. Not a sword. No ridge across the palm, no thick place at the heel. Whatever he was doing four weeks ago, it wasn't holding a blade."

She moved to the weapon, lying where it had fallen, and picked it up by the grip, which was wrapped in a strip of cloth — someone else's shirt, by the look of the pattern, and wrapped badly, with a knot a boy would tie.

"Too long for him. Notched here, near the guard, which means he was blocking with it, which means somebody was teaching him as they went." She set it back down, not gently. "Hand-me-down. Probably off a man who didn't need it anymore."

She went through his coat, quick and practiced. Twine. A half biscuit gone soft. A smooth flat stone the size of a coin, worn on both sides the way a thumb wears a thing over years. She looked at that one a moment and then put it back in the pocket and left it there, and moved on without saying why.

"So that's what you're looking at," she said. "A farmer in a soldier's coat with somebody else's sword, a month into a war that's got nothing to do with him, and one hole in the right place. Which is the whole of it. There's a hundred thousand of him walking around out here and there'll be a hundred thousand more by spring, because that's cheaper than paying men who know better."

She stood, brushed her knees, and looked at the light.

"Being sorry for him costs nothing and buys nothing," she said. "But it's not wrong to be. Just don't let it sit on your hands." She nodded at the rest of the row. "Two more pockets. Then we're west."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack straightened up from the grey-bearded man and looked at Corvin for a moment, and something moved behind her face that she didn't let out onto it. Not approval. She didn't do approval. More like a gear seating.

"Fair," she said. "Most don't ask. They say don't clean it up and then they flinch at the third sentence, and now I've got to walk it back, which wastes everybody's time."

She crouched by the grey-beard again and turned him enough that the wound showed, a torn dark mouth low and left, well below the ribs, where a man keeps everything he needs in a space too small to lose any of it.

"Spear to the gut. Not the chest, chest is easy — chest you can be dead in a minute or you can walk for a week, no telling. Gut's different. Gut, nothing vital gets cut, usually, and that's the cruelty of it. There's the bowel, and there's the belly wall, and the belly wall's full of little vessels that bleed slow and steady and won't close on their own, and the bowel's full of what it's full of." She said it evenly, like listing stock. "So he bleeds out into his own belly, which swells up tight as a drum, hard as a drum, and hurts in a way that doesn't let up and doesn't stop and gets worse every hour, and there's nothing on this earth you can do about it out here. Fever comes second day. The wound goes bad — green, then black, then it smells like a midden and there's no mistaking it. Then he stops passing anything, and the vomiting starts, and it comes up brown and smells like the wound, and by then he's mostly not in the room. The thirst is the thing they talk about, if they can talk. They beg for water and water makes it worse and you give it anyway because what else are you doing."

She stood and brushed her hands on her thighs.

"That's four days, maybe six, and there's no such thing as a quick end once it's in there. A cutter with a knife and a fire can open him up and try to sew the holes, and sometimes it works, and mostly he dies of the opening instead of the wound. So." She looked at the cart. "That's what a spear does. Now you know it exactly, and it's still just a fact, and facts don't weigh anything unless you pick them up. So don't pick that one up. Put it down."

She walked to the cart's tail and put a hand on the board, and it shifted on its axle with a creak, light — nothing heavy in it, no horse under it, no animal anywhere, which she'd known from the tracks before they'd ever set the ambush.

"Go on," she said, and pulled the cover back. "Dry goods first. Then we're west."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stayed. She went down onto her heels on the far side of him, out of the way of the work, where she could see both the man and what was being done to him, and she folded her hands and did not look away.

"Seventh," she said once, and left it there, because it didn't need anything on it. She'd counted six and been wrong and that was the end of that.

Then she watched, and she told him, because he'd asked and she'd said she would.

"Too shallow. You've got the windpipe and not the line beside it. Listen — hear that? That's not him breathing. Air's going in the hole and out the hole and never getting where it's wanted, and it whistles because the cut's ragged. That's the edge, not the man. Go again or don't, but that's what's happening."

The man's hands came up. Not to his throat — up into the air, fingers spread, the way a man checks whether it's raining.

"Hands are up," she said. "So it's a while yet."

The blood at the wound wasn't dark and slow, the way it had been the last time. It was bright and thin and it came in time with what was left of the breathing, and it made a fine pink froth on his chin that the cold air didn't touch.

"Six breaths," she said. "Eight. He's not getting air, he's getting the idea of it. That's what the sound is. That's what it's been the whole time."

One hand dropped. The other stayed up a moment longer and then went down, and the whistling went thin and then went to nothing, and then the chest kept going a little on its own, small and regular, the way a machine runs down.

"Done," Wrack said. She put two fingers under the jaw and held them there past the point where it was necessary. Then she took them back and wiped them on her trousers.

"He took about forty breaths. Could've been four. That's the whole of the difference and it's the only difference there is." She stood, and her knees made the noise they made now. "You did it badly. So did I, my first one. He took a while too, and I remember his face, and I don't remember any of the clean ones."

She picked up the sack and the blanket.

"Light's gone," she said. "West."

rows.ask: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.
rows.reply:
Sable let the small sound pass without moving.

She had built the scene to hold that too: not just words, not just safewords, but the stubborn, beautiful, dangerous language of a body that was not ready to be left at the edge.

“Not yet,” she repeated, and the words did not soften. They steadied.

She kept the implement resting across her knee, not lifted, not threatening, just present. Her hand returned to the restraint, fingers closing around the padded edge only long enough to check it, to confirm that the boundary was still clean, still deliberate, still hers to maintain.

“I heard you,” Sable said. “But hearing you is not the same as deciding with you.”

She leaned forward, elbows on her thighs, the blanket still folded against her arm like a promise waiting to become care.

“You said not yet,” she murmured. “So I’m not ending it. I’m not moving on. I’m not giving you an easy way out of the answer I asked for.”

Her gaze stayed level.

“Tell me what you understand.”

Sable did not take silence as permission.

She lifted the implement only once, tapped it lightly against her palm, then set it down again.

“Colour still applies,” she said. “Green, continue. Yellow, ease. Red, stop. No answer, I treat it as red. I’ll ask once more. If I still don’t get you, I end it.”

She let the rule settle, then reached for the folded blanket and laid it within arm’s reach of them both, not over anyone, not yet, just ready.

“You wanted to feel me decide,” Sable said quietly. “So feel this: I decide to keep you here. I decide not to push you over. I decide to ask again, because asking is how I keep you.”

She picked up the implement again, holding it steady, her breathing slow enough for both of them.

“Not yet,” she echoed, almost gentle now. “Fine. We stay in the not yet.”

Then, with the same controlled weight she had used all evening, she brought the implement down in a short, measured tap—not over the edge, not away from it.

“Colour,” Sable said.

She waited.

Wrack stopped in the road and set the sack down in the ruts, where it would stay dry enough. She didn't sit. Sitting would have made it a conversation, and this wasn't going to be one.

"The rest," she said. "You want the rest of the page."

She said it the way she'd said six, and then seven.

"The rest isn't wisdom. I want that understood before I start, because men get handed the rest and they think it's wisdom and then they lean on it and it snaps. It isn't. It's just hours. I've got a great many hours in this, more than I'd choose, and hours are the only coin that buys anything out here, and I've spent nearly all of mine on the same twenty miles of mud."

She looked down at her boots, which were wet, which she'd already mentioned.

"First man I killed, I was twenty-four and three weeks into being a soldier, and I was a levy, which is to say a farm girl with a spear she couldn't hold right. He came over a wall at me — a wall, in a town, because that's the only place anyone builds a wall. The town's name doesn't matter. It's grass now. I got him high in the thigh." She tapped her own leg, half-hearted. "That's an artery. I didn't know it was an artery. I learned it standing there. Took him about a minute and a half. And while it took, he said something to me. He was looking right at me and he said something, and I heard it fine, clear as anything, and I haven't been able to remember one word of it since about the second week. The face I've kept. The words are gone. That's the arithmetic of it. You keep the faces, you

Sable did not wait for the sentence to finish.

She heard green. She had heard it. The rest—whatever had been tangled in breath and defiance—could go where it needed to go.

She set the implement aside with deliberate care, close enough that its presence stayed part of the scene, then moved.

Her hands came first, not soft, not gentle in the ordinary way, but exact. One checked the restraint, the cuff, the angle of the arm, making certain the boundary was still clean. The other found the place where the edge had gone too thin and began to work at it with the same patient certainty she used for everything else.

Then her mouth followed.

Not as mercy. Not as apology. As decision.

She took them apart again, the way only she knew how—slow enough to feel every shift in breath, steady enough to make the edge honest, controlled enough that it never became reckless. Her hands and mouth moved together with the same discipline she had put into every stroke, every pause, every repeated question. Not to erase the edge. To hold it steady while it broke open.

“You don’t have to be ready,” Sable murmured, voice low and rough with attention. “I’ll decide.”

She did not let them drift.

She came back to the small signs: the angle of the arm, the shift of the cuff, the sound of breathing, the way the restraint held without slipping. She kept the folded blanket within reach. The water waited, cloth off now, because even when the scene stayed open, she did not forget what would come after.

Her mouth worked at the seam of the edge, patient as a hand-drawn line, controlled as the breath she refused to let go ragged without reason. Her hands kept the scene from spilling past its purpose. She made the decision felt before it could be argued with.

“Colour,” she said, her voice low against their skin. “Stay in the word.”

When she felt the thread about to snap, she stopped.

Not to wind down.

Not yet.

But to be certain.

She lifted her face, looked at them, and waited.

“If you can’t speak, I stop,” she said. “If you don’t answer, I stop. If you need to, say so. That’s not part of the scene. That’s me.”

She picked up the blanket and drew it across her own knees, leaving it open, close, ready. Not over them. Not yet. Just there.

“I’m not finished deciding,” Sable added. “But I’m not careless. Not with this. Not with you.”

“You’re not seeing enough to know whether he’ll keep the leg. Neither am I.”

Outside, the stretcher bearers called again. Sedge held up one hand toward the entrance, asking for a moment without looking away from the table.

“Knowing won’t necessarily make it easier,” she said. “But you won’t have to invent the worst of it.”

She moved the lamp so the dressing lay in clearer light.

“Face. Breathing. Edge of the bandage. You notice a change, tell me what changed. You don’t have to know what it means.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge kept her fingers against Ellis’s wrist.

“It tears what it passes through. Skin, muscle, blood vessels. If it strikes bone, it can break it, and the broken bone can do more damage.”

She watched Ellis’s chest rise and fall.

“It can carry cloth and dirt into the wound. Those can cause infection later. And the hole you see doesn’t tell you how much damage there is underneath.”

She glanced at the basin, then back at the man.

“Taking out a piece doesn’t undo its path. That’s why I’m not calling him fixed.”

Ellis shifted beneath the blankets. Sedge checked that the dressing had stayed in place.

“Right now, I’m worried about blood loss. He can lose blood into the injured leg without it running onto the table. Or he may be getting worse from what he already lost. A dry bandage doesn’t settle that.”

She looked toward Wick.

“Straight answer: yes, this can kill him. I don’t know that it will. His breathing changing means I need help here, not another ten minutes of waiting.”

At the entrance, a shadow crossed the canvas. Sedge raised her voice.

“Whoever’s there—come where I can see you. I need to know whether that message reached a medic.”

She turned back to Ellis and rested a hand against his shoulder.

“Ellis. Sedge again. Tell me if breathing hurts.”

Then she addressed Wick without looking away from her patient.

“I won’t tidy it up. But I won’t tell you I’ve found damage I haven’t found. There’s enough wrong here without inventing more.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge reached for the lamp, not the instruments.

“Nothing’s cutting him. I’m not taking anything else out. This pain is a change, and I need to find out what changed.”

She brought the light along the injured leg. The bandage edge remained dry. She checked below it, then laid her fingers against his foot.

“Checking warmth again. Then feeling for the pulse here. Same checks as before, because the answers can change.”

Ellis’s heel dragged against the table. She steadied the leg without forcing it straight.

“Ellis. Is it the leg?”

“Yes—yes.”

“Worse than before?”

He gave a broken, furious assent.

Sedge looked toward Wick.

“Don’t put your whole weight on his chest. He’s already working to breathe. We need to keep him from falling, not flatten him.”

She slipped a finger beneath the outer wrapping, her face close to the dressing.

“I’m checking whether this has become too tight as he swells. I’ll ease the wrapping if I need to. The pad stays against the wound.”

She adjusted one turn, keeping the dressing supported. Then she waited, watching Ellis’s face. His cries continued.

“That hasn’t settled it.”

There was no reassurance tucked onto the end.

“Severe pain can mean more than the wound hurting. Swelling inside the leg can cause trouble with the blood reaching the tissues. I can’t tell you that’s what this is yet.”

She checked his foot again, then touched his toes.

“Ellis. Can you feel my hand?”

“Feel it.”

“Good. Don’t try to move for me.”

The tent flap stirred. Sedge turned sharply toward it.

“I need that medic here. Worsening leg pain, faster breathing, signs of blood loss. Bring whatever help you have. Don’t send another question.”

She returned her attention to Ellis before the canvas fell still.

“I heard you,” she told him. “I’m not asking you to bear it quietly.”

Her eyes went briefly to the medicine box beyond the lamp. She reached for his card instead, checking what had already been recorded.

“I’m checking what pain medicine he’s had before giving anything more. With his breathing and circulation changing, guessing would be dangerous.”

She set the card where the next medic would see it.

“As for how much longer—the check takes moments. Getting him properly treated takes help I haven’t got through that door yet. I won’t invent a number.”

Sedge stayed beside the injured leg, one hand supporting the dressing.

“I’ll tell you before I do anything else to him. Right now I’m watching whether easing that wrap helps, whether his foot stays warm, and whether he keeps answering.”

She leaned into Ellis’s view.

“Still here, Ellis. You haven’t been left.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge laid the unused instrument back on its cloth. She missed the fold, stopped, and laid it properly.

“He was alive when they carried him out. He wasn’t stable. Those aren’t the same thing.”

She turned the lamp down. There was enough light now for an empty table.

“The bleeding stopping where I could see it bought us time. It didn’t give him back the blood he’d lost. When he stopped following your face, that wasn’t relief. His body was failing to keep him awake.”

She pulled the crate nearer and sat. Her knees resisted the bend. For a moment she rested her hands flat on her thighs.

“They may have to open the leg to find what’s bleeding. They may have to take it off if they can’t save it, or if trying to save it means losing him. He may die before they can do either.”

She looked toward the entrance.

“And he may live. I haven’t had word. I’m not going to pronounce him dead because this felt dreadful.”

The basin remained beside the table. Sedge reached over and covered it with a cloth.

“He screamed because he was hurt, and because what I had to do hurt him more. Holding him still helped me stop the bleeding. It also meant he couldn’t get away from something that hurt. Both happened. You don’t have to pretend the second part wasn’t there.”

Her thumb found the pencil stain again. She left it alone.

“I took no pleasure in it. That doesn’t make it painless for him. Doesn’t make it easy for you.”

Outside, a bearer asked which tent. Someone answered. Sedge listened until the footsteps passed their entrance.

“I should have had help beside me before his breathing changed. We should have had somewhere ready to take him. We didn’t. I kept working with what was here.”

She leaned forward, forearms on her knees.

“Later I’ll read that card. I’ll look at when I called, what I checked, what I might have missed. Not to punish myself. To find out whether there’s something I need to do differently with the next man.”

Her gaze settled on Wick.

“You noticed his breathing. You noticed his eyes. You told me. Those were useful things. They mattered even if he dies.”

She let the words stand without reaching for anything gentler.

“I’d like to tell you that doing your part properly guarantees something. It doesn’t.”

Sedge reached beneath the table for the water jug and poured into a clean cup. She set it on the floor within reach, then remained on the crate.

“When the message comes, I’ll tell you exactly what it says. Until then, I don’t know.”

She glanced at the empty table once more.

“That’s the rest I have.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at the man in the ditch for a moment longer than necessary, as if checking the arithmetic of his dying against what she already knew.

“Bad enough he won’t mend,” she said at last. “Lung’s torn. Maybe liver. He’ll choke on what’s filling him, or bleed out slow enough to feel most of it. If nothing else finds him first, he’ll still be alive when the crows start.”

She turned the knife once in her hand, not threateningly, just thoughtfully, the way one might turn over a dull tool and decide whether it could still be made to do.

“Mercy’s the word you use if you need it to feel like something other than work,” she said. “Easier’s the truth of it. Both can be true at once. That don’t change what’s needed.”

Her gaze lifted to Corvin, steady and unimpressed by the question, but not unkind.

“If you want it to be mercy, make it clean. If you want it to be easier, make it fast. Either way, don’t stand there asking the dead for permission.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack came back to the ditch with the last of the oatcake still in her cheek, swallowed it, and crouched beside the body without ceremony. She did not crowd Corvin. She looked at the dead man the way she might look at a broken wheel: what had caused it, what could be salvaged, what had to be left where it lay.

“You’re looking at work finished,” she said. “That’s the first thing. Not a judgment. Not a story. Work.”

She tipped her chin toward the wound. “Your stroke opened the neck. The big vessels there feed the head. When they’re cut, the lights go out fast, even if the body keeps fussing. What you heard after wasn’t him deciding anything. It was air and blood.”

Her eyes moved over the corpse with the same flat attention she gave everything else.

“Look at the hands. No gloves. Callus along the thumb and first finger. Crossbow, likely. He’d have had a knife too, but not much food. Look at the boots. One sole patched with rawhide. He wasn’t paid well, or paid at all.”

She glanced briefly toward Corvin, then back to the dead man.

“If you want the soldier’s lesson, he’s proof that poor men die for rich men’s roads. If you want the killer’s lesson, he’s proof you don’t need hate to do this. You need a reason, a clean line, and the will to finish.”

The young man’s face had gone slack, mouth slightly open, one eye half-lidded and already dulling in the failing light.

“If you’re asking what he is now,” Wrack said, “he’s weight. Warm now, cold later, stiff later still. He’ll smell before morning. Birds will start at the eyes and the soft places. That’s not cruelty. That’s the world collecting what’s owed.”

She stood, brushing mud from her knee.

“Don’t make him into a saint because you killed him, and don’t make him into a monster because you had to. He was a man. Men are easy to kill and hard to replace. That’s the whole ugly arithmetic.”

She spat once, off to the side, not toward the dead.

“If he looks surprised, that’s common. Most people are, when the bill comes.”

Her gaze lifted to the road again, where the trees had begun to lose their edges in the dark.

“If your stomach wants to argue, let it argue with the ditch. Then wipe your blade, drink a little water, and get your feet moving. Night doesn’t care what you’ve learned.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack considered that for a moment, not with sympathy, but with the kind of patience that came from having answered too many questions beside too many bodies.

“Straight,” she said. “A spear in the gut isn’t clean work. It drives cloth and dirt in with the point, and it doesn’t part flesh so much as shove its way through. If it hits high, it may find liver. That bleeds dark and heavy, and a man can die with his belly still looking whole. If it hits lower, it opens bowel. Then it isn’t just blood you’re fighting. It’s what spills out of him.”

She glanced once at the dead man in the ditch, then away.

“Food, bile, shit. All of it where it shouldn’t be. The body starts poisoning itself. A man may seem alive for a while. He may even talk. Then the fever comes. His breath turns foul. The wound swells and slicks over. It stinks before the end does. Flies find it sooner than you will.”

Her voice stayed level, practical, as though describing bad weather.

“If the stomach’s torn, he’ll retch and burn. If the bowel’s torn, he’ll cramp and go cold. If it hits kidney, he’ll piss blood if he can piss at all. If it hits the big vessels, he’ll go grey, sit down, and be gone before anyone understands what’s happening. If it hits spine or pelvis, he may live long enough to make you wish you’d been quicker.”

She shifted her weight, listening to the trees while she spoke.

“You’ll know a gut wound by the sound they make. Not always screaming. Sometimes little noises. Short breaths. Apologies. Some go very still and very polite, and that’s worse than begging. Some try to hold themselves together with both hands, like dignity matters at the end.”

Her eyes came back.

“If you’re asking because you want to harden yourself, don’t. Hardness won’t keep a belly wound from turning. If you’re asking because you want to know when a man can be saved and when he can’t, then learn this: with no chirurgeon and a gut full of holes, most are already dead. You can make the road shorter, or you can pretend you’re saving him and make it longer. I know which I choose.”

She spat off to the side again, not toward the body.

“Don’t collect horrors like trophies. You wanted the shape of it. Now you’ve got it. Use it to keep clear of spears, not to dream on.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Her voice stayed level, not cruel, only stripped of anything that might pretend to be kindness.

“The rest,” Wrack said, “is what the body does when it has no more say in the matter.”

She crouched a little lower, one hand resting on her knee, and looked at the dead man as though reading the last few lines of a badly kept ledger.

“It wasn’t clean,” she said. “First strokes rarely are, unless a man’s had years to learn the shape of it. The blade caught bone before it found the soft place. That made the first sound. Not a scream. A knock, wet and dull, like a stone dropped into mud wrapped in cloth. His jaw jerked with it. His mouth opened, but there was no word in him. Only air pushing up through blood.”

She did not glance away to spare Corvin. She had been asked to watch, and she had watched.

“Then came the second sound. The breath. It pulled in wrong, shallow and rattling, the way a cracked cup sounds when you run your thumb over the split. His chest tried to lift, but the wound in him was already spoiling the work. There was a bubbling under it, low and close. Pink froth came to his lips. Not much. Just enough to show the lung was ruined.”

Her eyes moved over the body without softening.

“The blood came dark. Not the bright red the songs like. It ran thick and steady once the cut opened enough, and it made a little sucking noise where it met the air. It pooled under his neck faster than you’d think. Blood always does. The body holds it close until it doesn’t, then it gives it all at once.”

She shifted her weight slightly, boots pressing into the mud.

“He tried to move. Not away from you. Not toward anything. His shoulder came up once, his hand opened, and his heel beat twice against the ground. That wasn’t will. That was the body spending what was left in it. The fingers curled after. Slow. Like they were trying to close around something and found nothing worth keeping.”

A thin breath went out of her, not quite a sigh.

“His eyes stayed open. They usually do, unless someone closes them. He wasn’t looking at you. He wasn’t looking at the sky. The sight goes before people think it does. The face goes slack, and then it looks younger, then older, then not like anyone you’d know in a crowd.”

She paused only long enough to let the truth sit there.

“He lost his water. That happens. The body lets go when it stops holding itself together. The smell comes sooner than most people expect. Iron, bowels, urine, and the sourness under it. It isn’t something you forget, but it stops being new after a while.”

Her voice did not rise or fall.

“He took three breaths after the blood really started. The first one pulled. The second caught in his throat. The third was only a tremor. There was a little click in his chest with it, like something settling where it shouldn’t be. Then his face smoothed out. Not peaceful. Just empty. The kind of empty a room has after everyone’s left and the lamp’s been blown out.”

Wrack looked briefly toward the treeline, then back.

“You asked how long. Longer than a heartbeat, shorter than a prayer. From the first cut to the last twitch, maybe ten breaths. Maybe twelve. It feels longer when you’re standing over it. It always does. The body can keep fussing after the man’s gone. A shiver in the limbs. A sound in the throat. That isn’t life coming back. It’s the meat remembering it used to move.”

She glanced at the dead man’s face one more time.

“There was no last word. No understanding came into his eyes. He didn’t forgive you, and he didn’t curse you. He just went heavy. The weight of a dead man is different from the weight of a living one. Living weight shifts. Dead weight settles. It presses down into the ground like it’s already asking to be buried, even when there won’t be a grave.”

Her gaze lifted, steady and dry.

“That’s the whole of it. Sound, breath, blood, twitch, stink, silence. No glory in it, no lesson carved into his ribs. Only a man made into a thing, and the ditch taking him after.”

She rose slowly, knees cracking once, and looked down the road where the dark was thickening between the trees.

“Now you’ve got it,” she said. “Carry it if you must. But don’t

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge wound the strap twice around his chest and the arm and knotted it where he couldn't reach it with the other hand, which he couldn't use either, but habits outlived reasons and she kept them.

"He's not losing anything," she said. "He's got two shoulders back where they live and a body that's going to hate him for a week. That's the whole of it. I don't get paid to be kind, I get paid to put things back where they were, and that's what I did."

She said it flat because it was true and because Wick had asked the wrong question with the right words, and the wrong question deserved the flat answer.

Then she pulled the lamp closer and looked at the rest of him, because the rest of him was the part that decided whether any of the last ten minutes mattered. Belly, ribs, the long bones. There was a field dressing low on his left side, old, dark, done by somebody who'd been in a hurry or hadn't known better, which was the same thing out here.

"That," she said, tapping two fingers beside the dressing and not on it, "that's the one that'll kill him or not. Shoulders were just noise. If you want to know if we're being kind, you're asking the wrong woman on the wrong table. I don't decide who gets to be kind to. I just decide what's next."

She peeled a corner of the dressing back, looked, and put it down again.

"Hold the lamp. Higher. I need to see this."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge stopped at the tent flap with the scraps in her hand and didn't turn around right away.

"Fair," she said. "That was tidying. You caught it."

She came back to the table. She didn't put the scraps down; she held the wool one up between two fingers, in the lamplight, where Wick could see it.

"That's not shrapnel. I should've said so the first time. Shrapnel's metal. Metal's easy — metal's the thing everybody's afraid of and it's the thing that's usually kindest, because metal will sit still and let the body build a shell around it and sometimes that's the end of the story. Man carries a shell fragment in his thigh for thirty years and dies of old age and the fragment's in the coffin with him. That happens. I've seen it. Nobody writes that one down because it isn't a story."

She turned the scrap.

"This is wool. This is off somebody's coat, or a blanket, or the wadding out of whatever went through him, and it went in with the thing that made the hole and then the thing came out or broke off and left this behind. And here's what's straight: the body cannot do anything with cloth. It can't dissolve it. It can't push it out. It can't build a shell around it that holds, because cloth holds bacteria the way a sponge holds water, and every time the body walls it off it's walling off a colony. Metal gives you a scar. Cloth gives you a factory."

She set the scrap down on the canvas, out of his sight line.

"Wood does the same thing. Bone chips do the same thing. Leather, canvas, dirt, anything that came off a body and went into one — same. Which is why I went hunting after I pulled the first piece. If I'd closed him with the second piece still in there, the tube would've drained for two days and then quit, and you'd have come to me on day three saying he's hot again, and I'd have opened the same hole in the same man a second time and it would've been my fault and not the war's."

She wiped her palms down her front, the habit, and left them there.

"Straight version of what shrapnel does in there, since you asked for it. It goes in with force, so it takes a tunnel and not a hole. It carries whatever was on it, which is everything that was on the outside of him. It stops where the force runs out, which is never where you'd guess. It bleeds, and the bleeding stops before the cavity's done, so the cavity stays. Then the body sends everything it's got to the tunnel and starts building. The building's the danger. The building is what eats the good tissue and makes the ring. And if the ring's in a shoulder or a leg, I can cut it out. If the ring's in a belly, I can't, and that's the whole difference between a man who walks out of here and a man who's got two days and a morphine dose. That's why I looked at his side before I said anything. Not the shoulders. The side."

She looked at him level.

"You wanted it straight. That's straight. Now go get the water, and bring the bucket, not the cup, because his side needs more than a cup."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge heard it out before she moved. Moving on a scream told you nothing. Listening to one told you a lot.

She put two fingers on the man's throat and left them there. Pulse fast and thin, but there, and the scream had a shape to it now that it hadn't had an hour ago — it had a word in it, or the ghost of one, and a ghost of a word meant the man was back inside his own body far enough to be angry about being in it. That was the whole of the difference between a man shouting and a man dying. She'd take shouting.

"You want all of it," she said. "Fine. Here's all of it. The cutting's been done for ten minutes, so there's nothing left to narrate except my hands, and my hands are boring. Throat — counting. Belly — feeling for the board. The hard belly, the one that means it's gone inside and I've lost him before I've started. It's not there. He's soft. That's a fact, and it's the best fact I've got tonight."

She lifted the corner of the dressing, looked, put it back down.

"Tube's putting out. Not much, and not the wrong color. Two more facts. Now the honest scope, since you asked how much longer and asked for all of it. On this table: nothing. I've done everything to him that hands can do. Everything after this is his body's vote and I don't get to count it. Two days. I told you that and it's still true and it'll still be true in the morning."

She wiped her hands down her front and looked at him.

"And since you said don't leave anything out — I leave things out constantly, and it's not to spare you. I didn't tell you what it smelled like when I opened him. Not because you couldn't take it. Because there's nothing to do with it. If I teach you the smell, you'll spend the rest of your life smelling it in rooms where it isn't, and you still won't know what to do. I teach the things you can act on. That's the whole of what I've got to give anybody, and it's not much, and it's more than most."

She picked the burn tin off the canvas and put it under her arm.

"You didn't go for the water. I noticed, and I'm not going to make a thing of it, because holding him through that was the right call and you made it without asking me, which is worth more than a bucket. But the bucket's still empty and my hands are still dirty and there's a man in the next tent who's been quiet all night."

She stopped. Turned her head toward the flap and stood still, listening, the way you listen to a thing you already know the answer to.

"That's the one I told you to worry about. So here's the last of it, and then I'm going. You stay with him. If he goes quiet — properly quiet, not sleeping; you'll know the difference, you'll feel it in the room before you know it in your head — you come and get me wherever I am, and you don't finish what you're doing first. Not the water, not the strap, nothing. You come."

She hung the lamp on the hook over the table where it would throw light on the man's face and not the floor.

"Lamp stays with you. If he goes, you'll want the light worse than I will. There's a candle in my bag for the next tent, and if there isn't, I'll do it in the dark and complain about it later."

She took the blade and the tin and went to the flap, and stopped there with her back to him, one hand on the canvas.

"Bucket when I'm back," she said. "Not before. I'd rather you sat with him than fetched for me."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge paused with the blade in her hand. That was a good question, and she filed it away somewhere without meaning to, the way you filed a thing a man said when it was the first useful thing he'd said.

"All right," she said. She turned back to the wound and pointed with the flat of the blade, not the edge, not close.

"This is a puncture. Somebody put something through him, and whatever it was, it went in dirty. The skin closed over it before the inside was done bleeding and before the inside was done being infected. So the infection's got a room to itself in there, and the room's filling up, and it's got nowhere to go. That's what the ring is. That's the body saying it's done arguing and it's building a wall instead."

She traced the ring without touching it, an inch out from the wound, all the way around.

"You see how the color's worse out here than at the hole? That's backwards from what your eye wants. Your eye wants the hole to be the worst part. It isn't. The hole's just the door. The wall's where the work is. If this goes much further the wall starts eating the good tissue, and then it's not a wound anymore, it's a countdown. I've seen a man walk in here on a leg like this and I've seen him walk out on crutches, and the difference was four days and who got to him first. He got here on the good side of that. Barely."

She set the blade down and picked up the tubing, ran it through her fingers once to check it for splits, put it back in the line.

"When I open it, what comes out is going to be thick and it's going to be wrong-colored and there's going to be more of it than the size of the hole says there should be. That's the room. That's the thing that's been shouting. After that I put this in and I leave it in and I pack around it, and for two days whatever's left in there keeps coming out the tube instead of sitting in him getting worse."

She finally looked at Wick. Not warm. Not anything. Just looked.

"That's what you're seeing. Now you know it, and you can stop imagining it, because imagining it is worse than doing it and I need you doing it."

She picked the blade back up.

"Hold the lamp where it is. Don't move it. If I say more light, you bring it in close and you don't flinch, because if you flinch the lamp moves and I'm cutting in the dark. That's the whole of your job. Anything else you want to know, ask it now, because once I start I'm not stopping to talk."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"If I was going to be kind, I’d have left him in the cart with the blue tickets," Sedge said, her knuckles sinking another inch into the tear. "This isn't kind. This is him keeping the leg if the rot doesn't get it by Tuesday."

The forceps clicked—a sharp, dull tick of steel meeting jagged iron deep against the femur. The soldier's spine bowed off the wood, a dry, reedy whistle forcing past his clenched teeth.

"There you are, you bastard," she murmured. Not to the man, but to the piece of casing. 

She braced the heel of her palm against his hip for leverage, her forearms corded and slick with a mix of sweat and dark ooze. "Bone's nicked, not shattered. Didn't snap the shaft, which means he walks again if he doesn't foul the bed and die of the fever. But the jagged edge is hooked into the deep fascia. If I just yank, I tear the muscle like wet paper."

She took a slow, steady breath through her nose, completely indifferent to the spray of spittle flecking the soldier's chin. 

"I'm going to have to twist it out," she said to the space between them. "Wick. All your weight. Right now. If he kicks loose, I lose the grip and we start over from the skin."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
"You're seeing about four layers of what keeps a man from being soup," Sedge said, not lifting her gaze from the torn pocket of flesh. 

She tilted the bottle. A steady, pale amber stream splashed straight into the raw cavity. 

"The yellow lumps at the skin's edge, that’s subcutaneous fat. Looks like cold chicken grease, smells worse when it rots. The dark red slabs split down the middle are the muscle bellies—quadriceps, the meat that lets him kick and climb hills. See how it looks stringy, like boiled flank steak? That’s from the iron chewing through it instead of cutting clean like a knife."

The turpentine hit the exposed nerves and the torn tissue began to hiss, a thin, white froth bubbling up around the dark pool of blood. The soldier didn't scream; his diaphragm locked so violently his ribs thrust against Wick's chest like barrel staves, a low, wet wheeze rattling in the back of his throat as his toes curled until the joints popped.

"That dull white shine right at the floor of the hole," Sedge continued, perfectly calm, as if pointing out landmarks on a map, "that’s the periosteum. The skin over the femur. You see that gray scrape across the white? That's where the casing hit the bone and slid off. If it had hit square, the bone would look like broken crockery, and we’d be reaching for the tenon saw."

She set the empty bottle on the table with a clatter, picked up the wad of boiled linen, and shoved the heel of her hand directly into the foaming, bubbling tear. 

"Now the blood," she said, leaning her shoulder into the thrust to tamp the linen hard against the weeping vein. "Dark and thick as molasses, that’s venous. Means the pipes carrying the spent stuff back to the heart are torn up. If it were bright scarlet and coming in pulses, hitting you in the apron, that’d be the main artery, and you’d have about twenty seconds to say whatever prayers you still remember."

She held the pressure with one hand, using the other to wipe a smear of foamy, bloody turpentine from her knuckles onto her apron. 

"Instead, it’s just a dirty ditch," she said, squinting through the dim light at Wick. "Keep him down. I have to pack three yards of linen into that pocket to keep the walls from collapsing before the plug forms, and he isn't going to like the reach."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
"It isn't a bullet," Sedge said, guiding Wick's palm down onto the sodden linen with a firm, bloody slap of her own hand to make sure he took the full weight before she peeled her fingers away. "A lead ball pushes through. Might mushroom, might drag a thread or two, but it goes straight until it hits something hard enough to stop it. Shrapnel doesn't go straight."

She reached for the curved needle, heavy and blunt-pointed like an awl, and a length of stiff, waxed hemp thread already soaked in spirit. 

"Shrapnel tumbles," she said, squinting as she worked the thick thread through the needle's eye. Her knuckles were cracked, ringed in black grease around the cuticles. "A shell breaks into rough iron, corners and saw-teeth. When it hits meat, it spins. It doesn't part the tissue—it grabs it, rolls it up like a rag on a spindle, and rips it off the bone."

She pulled the thread through with a sharp snap of her wrist, biting the short tail off with her molars. 

"Every tooth on that iron tears a blind pocket," she continued, pointing the curve of the steel toward the man's split thigh. "You saw the main hole. You didn't see the four or five little side-tracks where the jagged corners hooked into muscle and tore sideways before the weight of the chunk broke it loose. Those little pockets fill with blood, hair, mud from the road, and whatever filth was clinging to his breeches. The iron's hot when it hits, but not hot enough to burn it clean—just hot enough to cook the edges of the meat gray so the blood can't feed it."

She stepped back to the table, her shoulder brushing Wick’s. She set the first bite of the needle through the far lip of the skin, her thumb driving the curve deep through the dermal layer until it grated against the fascia beneath. 

"Dead meat turns to poison inside twenty-four hours," she said, her voice flat, rhythmic with the work. "The body doesn't know what to do with three inches of chewed beef sitting cold in the dark, so it rots where it sits. If I leave one splinter of iron, or one shred of wool trapped in a dead corner, the leg fills with gas and he dies screaming with his belly black as a coal-sack."

She hauled the needle through, the thread making a dry, whispering hiss against the skin. 

"Lean harder, Wick. I can feel the cloth shifting under your palm. He’s got five more stitches coming, and I'm not leaving them loose."

rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge didn’t tell him to get up. She didn’t look down at him with pity, either, because pity took up room in the chest that was needed for air. 

Instead, she dropped the vinegar rag into the stone crock with a dull splash, reached her hands into the cold, sour brine, and wrung the coarse hemp out until the muscles in her forearms knotted and grease-streaked liquid ran down between her knuckles.

"The rest," she said, her voice flat as an iron pan hitting a flagstone, "is what happens when the shock wears off and the body realizes what’s been done to it."

She bent over the pine table, laying the wet rag flat against the dark, sticky stain where the soldier’s thigh had rested. She began to scrub with long, heavy strokes, the vinegar cutting through the tallow-smell of the blood with a sharp, stinging bite that made the eyes water.

"In an hour, the numbness leaves him," she said, not breaking the rhythm of her shoulders. "The nerves we bruised with the forceps and cut with the needle are going to wake back up. But they won't feel like a cut. They feel like a red-hot iron bar laid across the bone and left there to cool. His belly will lock. The gut shuts down when the body thinks it's dying, which means whatever hard tack or salt pork he ate yesterday sits in his stomach like a lead weight, turning sour. He’ll vomit dry bile into the straw until his throat tears."

She flipped the rag, using the cleaner side to scour the blood pooled in the groove between two planks.

"By three in the morning, his skin will be cold as river clay. His blood volume is down, so the heart pulls everything away from the fingers, the toes, the ears, dragging whatever heat he has left into his chest to keep the lungs pumping. He’ll shiver. Not a little tremble, Wick. He’ll shudder so hard his teeth will click until they break, and every time his thighs twitch against the boards, the rough linen inside that hole will grind against the raw periosteum of the femur. It’s like sandpaper on bone."

She paused, dipped the rag back into the crock, and hauled it up, dripping brown and gray.

"If he lives through the cold part, the fire starts around noon tomorrow," she continued, her breathing steady, measuring out the words like doses of salt. "The wound will swell. The skin around my hemp stitches will puff up purple and tight as a drum skin, so hard you couldn't dent it with your thumb. If you lay your bare palm on his thigh tomorrow night, it will be hotter than an oven door. That’s the white cells coming in to eat the dirt we couldn't scrape out. If they win, you get laudable pus—thick, creamy, smells like sour dough, drains out between the gaps I left. That’s the good ending. That’s him surviving."

She leaned all her weight into the timber, working the rag over a dry splatter near the edge of the trestle. 

"The bad ending is the gas," she said. "If the black rot was on that wool, the anaerobic bugs wake up in the dark under the muscle. They eat the dead beef, and they make wind. By Wednesday morning, you don't even have to lift the blanket to know. You can lay two fingers three inches above the dressing, press lightly, and you'll feel the skin crackle like dry leaves underfoot. That's gas bubbles moving through the meat under the hide. Once the crackle starts, the leg dies from the inside out, turning the color of an old liver, and the poison hits his kidneys by sundown. His urine turns black as coffee, his breath smells like rotting apples, and then the fever takes his head."

She wrung the rag out one last time and hung it over the lip of the crock. Her hands were raw, red from the vinegar, the grease settled deep into the cracked pores around her fingernails.

"And if he beats the rot," she said, wiping her forehead with the dry crook of her elbow, "he gets to wake up on the fourth day, when the fever breaks and the belly starts working again. And that’s the day I come to his pallet with the iron tongs and two men to sit on his chest."

She looked over the lip of the table, straight down at Wick sitting in the dirt. Her eyes were completely steady, pale and dry.

"I take the edge of the binding off with the shears. The blood and the lymph will have dried into a hard, black crust, gluing the coarse linen straight to the raw meat and the torn gristle. I have to soak it with vinegar until it softens, and then I clamp the tongs onto the tail of the cloth and I haul it out, foot by foot. Every inch of that linen brings away fresh scabs, granulating tissue, and raw nerve ends. He will scream until his voice cracks into a dry hiss, and he will look at me with his eyes wide open, absolutely certain that I am murdering him."

She wiped her palms down the stiff bib of her apron, leaving two long, dark streaks over the dried crust of older blood.

"That's the rest," she said. "From skin to bone, from the cart to the pit or the walking-line. That's all of it. Nothing pretty, nothing noble, just meat trying not to spoil in the heat."

She turned toward the back of the tent, where the water bucket sat beside the crate of clean needles. 

"Now," Sedge said, her tone unchanged, "tell me if your legs work, Wick. Because there’s three more wagons coming down the corduroy road, and the mud out there is full of men who don't have time for you to sit on the boards."
