rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at the leg as if it had been introduced late to a room it did not belong in. The man had been shouting about his shoulders, and she had let the leg wait because the shoulders were nearer the lungs and the neck and were easier to kill him with.

“Neither,” she said. “That’s not the question.”

She took the shears and cut the trouser leg open from the hem up, not gently, because cloth soaked through with blood does not come off gently. The leg beneath was swollen, hot, and wet in a way that had stopped being rain. Sedge pressed two fingers above the knee and felt for the pulse there. She did it quickly, because slow examination is what you do when you have time and clean linen, and neither of those things had been seen in this tent for months.

“The foot is warm,” she said. “That is not kindness. That’s plumbing. The leg is still being fed.”

She pressed the wound with a folded gauze pad and watched the blood move through it. It was fast, but not spurting. Not yet.

“If he loses the leg, it will not be because I was cruel,” she told the tent. “It will be because the leg is already too far gone to stay attached to a body that won’t stop moving. If he keeps the leg, it will not be because I was kind. It will be because I stopped the bleeding and he didn’t die of something else first.”

She unwound a bandage and started wrapping the wound over the gauze, pulling it tight enough to hold pressure and not tight enough to strangle the limb. Her hands moved by themselves, counting the layers, checking the edge, making sure the bandage did not slip when the man’s leg twitched.

“This is bad enough to need a tourniquet if the pulse changes,” she said. “It isn’t bad enough yet for me to take the leg off. If it gets worse, I’ll do what the wound says, not what the man would prefer.”

She set the shears aside and wiped her hands on a rag that had already been dirty before she started. There was no clean rag anywhere.

“Ask me if he’s stable, and I’ll tell you he’s not,” Sedge said. “Ask me if he’s going to keep the leg, and I’ll tell you I don’t know. Ask me if this is kind, and I’ll tell you kind is the thing we don’t have time to feel while he’s on the table.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge did not offer a warning about looking. She moved the lamp to the crate beside the table so the light came down across the leg instead of across his face, then took the edge of the bandage between thumb and forefinger.

“You’re seeing what I’m seeing,” she said. “Good.”

She peeled the wrap back just far enough to expose the wound again. The blood had made a small dark flower in the center of the gauze and stopped there. Underneath, the leg was swollen tight and hot to the touch, the skin pulled shiny over the muscle. A jagged line ran down the outside of the calf, not deep enough to see bone, but wide enough to show where the cloth and dirt had been driven in by the blast.

“The bright red is blood,” Sedge said, pointing with the tip of her thumb without pressing. “The dark red is muscle. The yellow is fat. The grey threads are cloth from his trousers. I do not like the cloth. Cloth is a way for infection to walk inside him. But infection is later.”

She turned the gauze pad over and showed the underside. The blood had soaked through in a pattern that spread from the middle and faded at the edges.

“This is bleeding under pressure,” she said. “Not the kind that is killing him now. If it spreads past the bandage and the foot goes cold, I tie the tourniquet. If the foot stays warm and the bleeding stays where it is, I wash what I can reach, close what I can close, and pray the rest of his body does what it is supposed to do.”

She set the pad aside and lifted the foot, moving the toes one by one. They were slow, stiff, but they answered. The nail beds came pale under her press and pink again after.

“The foot is alive,” Sedge said. “That is the only part of this that is simple. A leg can be ugly and still live. A leg can be clean and still die if the blood stops coming.”

She let the foot fall back onto the table and rewound the bandage with firm, even turns.

“If you imagine it,” she told Wick, “you will make it worse than it is. This is not a story. It is a leg with dirt in it and blood trying to clot. I do not take pleasure in opening it, and I do not feel pity when I close it. I look for what is broken, what is bleeding, and what can be saved. That is all there is.”

When the bandage was done, she pressed two fingers into the pulse above the ankle and counted without moving her mouth.

“He keeps the leg unless the leg stops feeding,” she said. “Or unless he dies of something else first.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge did not tidy it. She pulled the edge of the bandage back with two fingers and kept it there, because the leg was the lesson and the lesson was easier when it was visible.

“Shrapnel is a bad name for most of it,” she said. “A shell goes off, and pieces of the shell, the ground, and his own trousers come into the leg with it. That is what people call shrapnel. It does not slice like a knife. It slams. Metal moves too fast for the body to make a clean cut. It tears muscle, pushes fat aside, cracks bone, and carries filth deep enough that the skin can close over it and pretend the work is done.”

She moved her thumb along the wound without pressing into it.

“Here, the piece came in low and slow enough not to shred the whole calf. It made a ragged channel. The bright edges are torn muscle. The pale bits are fat and cloth. The cloth worries me. Cloth is not blood. Cloth stays there, and bacteria ride on it like passengers on a cart. That is how a leg that looks stable becomes a leg that smells like death in two days.”

She let the bandage fall back into place.

“If the fragment had been faster, you would not have seen a neat wound. You would have seen a hole the size of a fist, with the rest of the leg bruised from the shock of it. Vessels that look intact can be bruised inside. Bones can split from the force even if the metal never touched them. The leg swells from the inside, and the swelling can choke off its own blood.”

Sedge picked up the gauze and began wrapping again, firm and even.

“That is what shrapnel does in there. It makes a mess that is not proportional to the hole. It steals blood, steals time, and leaves dirt behind. My job is not to make it sound less ugly. My job is to know which part is bleeding now, which part will infect later, and which part is already dead whether we admit it or not.”

She tied the bandage off and laid her palm near the knee.

“Right now, this leg is alive and contaminated. That is straight enough.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge did not tell him to stop screaming. Screaming was information. It meant the airway was open, the lungs were moving, and the man still had enough breath to fight with. It also meant she could not hear the other sounds, which was annoying.

She moved to the head of the table and stood close enough to smell the sour sweat on the man’s skin. The lamp swung, throwing the whole scene into restless shadow.

“I am listening for wet,” Sedge said. “Not for the scream. The scream is loud. The wet is quieter. If he cannot clear his mouth, he can die in the same bed he is screaming in.”

She lifted his eyelid with two fingers and checked the white of the eye, then the pupil. She did not shine the lamp directly into his face. She moved it to the side and watched how the pupils answered.

“Both small. Both even,” she said. “That is not perfect. That is not a reason to relax. That is one fewer hole in the bad picture.”

She leaned close to his mouth and listened again, then put one ear near his chest and counted breaths in her head while she watched the rise and fall under the blanket.

“Breath is fast,” she said. “Air is moving. No sucking sound. No rattle like he is drowning in his own spit. That is good enough for this minute.”

Then she moved down to the shoulders, keeping Wick’s weight in sight but not asking him to release. She did not trust the shoulders yet. Screaming could mean a man was terrified. It could also mean something had slipped back out of place under the strain of being held.

“I am checking the right,” Sedge said. “I am putting my thumb in front of the joint and my finger behind the bone. I am not twisting. I am not testing him for fun. I am looking for the gap that says the ball has left the cup.”

She pressed once, firmly, then shifted to the left.

“Right is seated. Left is seated. If he is screaming because the shoulders came out again, I would feel it. I do not. So this is not a shoulder problem anymore.”

She moved down the table to the leg, keeping one hand on the man’s wrist so she could feel the pulse while she worked. Her fingers were stained with blood and sweat, and she did not wipe them again. There was nothing clean to wipe them on.

“I am looking at the bandage line,” she said. “I drew it with charcoal. If the blood crosses the line, it moved. If it does not, it may still be moving underneath, but not enough to say so out loud yet.”

She peeled back the edge of the wrap just far enough to see the stain. It had darkened, but the charcoal mark held.

“It is not spreading,” she said. “That is not good news. That is only not bad enough to make me tie the tourniquet this second.”

She pressed two fingers behind the knee, then over the ankle, counting. Her lips moved once, then stopped.

“Pulse is faster,” she said. “Foot is still warm. Capillary refill is slow. Skin is cool and damp. That is shock. That is his body trying to keep the important parts alive by pulling blood away from the parts that can spare it.”

She looked at Wick, briefly, and not for permission.

“I am going to press his belly,” Sedge said. “He may not like it. He is already screaming. I do not have time to wait for him to decide.”

She slid one hand under the blanket and pressed flat against the abdomen, slow and steady, not poking. She moved from side to side, then up under the ribs, then down toward the hips, watching the man’s face as much as her hand.

“If it is soft, he may be in pain and frightened. If it is hard, he may be bleeding where I cannot see. If he has a rigid belly and a fast pulse and cold skin, I am not going to be nice about the next thing I do.”

She pulled her hand back and wiped it on the rag again, though the rag had stopped being a rag some hours ago and had become only another thing soaked in worse things.

“Belly is soft,” she said. “That is not a promise. That is not proof. It is only what I can feel while he is fighting me. I will check it again after the screaming stops. Or after he vomits. Or after he dies. Whichever comes first.”

She took the cup of water from beside the table and moved it farther away.

“No water,” she said. “Not while he is screaming. Not while I do not know whether he can swallow. A cup of kindness is a cup of death if it goes down wrong.”

She checked the straps at the shoulders, then the towel over his eyes, then the bandage on the leg, in that order. Her hands moved without hesitation, because hesitation was a luxury for places with lamps that did not swing and tables that did not shake.

“I am putting the time back down,” she said, taking the charcoal again and writing beside the line on the bandage. “Five minutes. If the blood crosses it by then, I know it moved. If it does not, I will still check it again in five minutes. That is not waiting. That is not watching him rot. That is measuring.”

She set the charcoal down and looked at the man’s hand, the one that had been gripping the towel after the shoulder went back in. It was slack now, fingers half curled.

“I am not giving him the pain medicine yet,” Sedge said. “I have it. I am looking at it. I am not giving it. If he is bleeding inside, the pain is the only alarm bell left. If I take it away and his breathing slows, I have traded his warning for my comfort. I do not get to do that.”

She paused, then said, quieter, “Not yet.”

She moved back to his head and put one hand near his mouth, feeling for breath, watching for spit and blood.

“I am watching for vomit,” she said. “If he vomits, he has to turn. Not the whole body. The head, mostly. If you twist him wrong with two freshly set shoulders, I will have to do it again, and you will have to do it again, and neither of us will thank the other for it.”

She looked at Wick’s shaking hands, then at the man’s throat, then at the leg again.

“How much longer?” Sedge said, answering him as if the question were a tool she had to pick up and use. “This check? Five minutes. If the bandage spreads, I stop asking and start tying. If the foot goes cold, I start counting toward something worse. If he keeps screaming and his pulse keeps climbing and his skin keeps cooling, I have to decide whether the screaming is pain or the body going out of order. That decision may take ten minutes. It may take until the ambulance comes. It may take until he stops being a patient and becomes a body.”

She said it flatly, without dressing it.

“I do not know how long he has,” she said. “I know how long I have to watch him. That is all anyone gets in a tent like this.”

She laid one hand over his heart, not to listen, but to feel the speed of it under the ribs.

“I am still here,” she told the man, though he could not hear her over his own screaming. “I am still checking. I am not leaving because you are making noise. I am not pretending you are better than you are. I am not going to take the leg off because it is ugly. I am not going to let you die because it is easier to be frightened than to work.”

She moved the tourniquet closer to her left hand, where she could reach it without looking. She moved the shears and the pressure bandage into the same place. She arranged them as if they were already waiting for orders.

“I am going to keep talking,” Sedge said. “Not because it helps him. Because it keeps me honest. If I stop saying what I am doing, I start saying what I want to be true. And what I want to be true is not in this tent.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren straightened. It was not a large movement. She had been standing correctly already, but there was a difference between standing correctly and standing for the record, and the witnesses would know it when they saw it.

So Del knew the form. She had wondered. Some seconds did not, and had to be prompted, and the prompting was its own small indignity that she had never found a way to spare them. He had asked his question first, as was his right, and now he had closed the questioning, and what came next was the account as it would be kept. The questions were permitted before this and not after. That was the reason for the order. A man was entitled to test the account, and then he was entitled to have it fixed.

"Witnessed," she said, and the three on her left answered it, one after another, low.

"I am Auren. This morning at the appointed hour I met him at this ground under the code, with seconds present and witnesses standing. In the third exchange he offered a high cut and I did not take it. On his recovery his weight was forward and his left foot was late. I stepped inside his line and put the point in beneath the right side of the jaw, above the collar, angled upward, to the depth of two inches or something more. The steel passed through the great vessel of the neck and did not go through. I withdrew it. He stood for the length of one breath and did not speak. He went to his knees and then onto his right side and he was dead before I had lowered my blade. I believe there was little pain. I do not claim there was none."

She did not look at the ground this time. The account was not for the ground.

"I saw the fault in his foot in the first exchange and again in the second, and I waited for it. I did not make the opening. I found it, and I had been looking. If I had taken the high cut he would have lived through the third exchange, and I believe I would have found the same fault in a later one. That is my judgement and I give it as judgement, not as fact."

Her sleeve had gone dark and stiff to the wrist. It was on the record now with the rest of it.

"That is the wound. That is the death. I have spoken it plain to his second, and his second has heard it, and you have heard that it was given." She turned her head, once, to the witnesses, and back to Del. "It is spoken. It is done."

The witnesses answered again, and then there was nothing more that the code required of her, and she stood with her hands at her sides and let the quiet come, and did not fill it.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren did not answer at once, and the pause was not hesitation. It was the code, which she was consulting in the way she consulted it, silently and without needing to look anything up.

"The account is spoken," she said. "It cannot be amended after the witnessing, and I would not amend it if it could. But there is nothing in the code that forbids the same words being said a second time, and I told you before the closing that I would say them again if you asked. You asked late. I do not think the lateness matters. I will not stand on it."

She looked to the witnesses, two of whom had taken a step toward the edge of the ground, and said, "Hold." They stopped. The one nearest turned back fully. She waited until all three were still and facing her, because a thing said plainly to an empty ground was not the thing Del had asked for.

Then she raised her right hand, the one with the stiffened cuff, and put two fingers to her own throat.

"Here." Her fingertips rested just below the angle of the jaw on the right side, above where a collar would sit, in the soft place before the bone. "Beneath the jaw, the right side, his right. Above the collar. The point went in here and travelled upward, toward the base of the skull, not across. Two inches, a little more. It did not come out anywhere. There was one wound and it was this one."

She held her hand there long enough for anyone to see exactly where, and then lowered it.

"It opened the great vessel that runs up the side of the neck. That is what killed him. Not the depth. Not the steel in the throat. The vessel." She said it evenly. "If the point had gone in a finger's width forward, it would have missed the vessel and found the windpipe, and he would have died more slowly and worse, and I would be standing here telling you that instead. It did not. It went where I put it. I am not asking you to be grateful for that. I am telling you it is so."

The witnesses had not moved. She released them with a small motion of the hand, and they began to go, and she let them.

"That is where it landed. It is the same place I told you the first time and the same place I told the record. If you want to see the mark itself before he is taken from the ground, that is your right as second, and no one here will stop you or think less of you for looking, or for not looking." She let her hands settle again at her sides. "I would look, if I were you. I have found that the thing a man imagines is usually larger than the thing that is there, and it is better to carry the true one."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren did not remind him that the code was finished with them both. He knew it. He had said the closing words himself, and he had heard her say that it was done, and he was asking anyway, and she had decided some time ago on a different ground with a different second that when a man asked a fourth time it was not because he had failed to hear the first three.

"Precisely, then," she said. "As exact as I have it. Where I am not certain I will say so."

She did not put her hand to her throat this time. He had seen the place.

"The point went in through the skin beneath the angle of the jaw and through the thin sheet of muscle that lies just under the skin there. That is nothing. A finger's depth. Below that, on that side of the neck, there is a bundle that runs up from the chest to the head, and it lies in a sheath of its own, and in it are the great artery that carries blood to the brain, the great vein that carries it back, and the cord of nerve that goes with them. They run together. You cannot reach one without reaching the others."

Her voice was level and did not hurry.

"The blade entered that sheath. It cut the artery across, or near enough across that the difference does not signify. It opened the vein alongside it. I cannot tell you what it did to the nerve and I will not guess. The angle was upward, toward the base of the skull, so the point passed behind the corner of the jaw and did not go across toward the windpipe. It did not enter the throat. It did not reach the spine. It stopped in the muscle at the back of the neck, or a little before that. I felt it stop and I withdrew."

She paused, because the next part was what the blade had done and not merely where it had gone, and that was what he had asked.

"When the artery was cut, the blood that should have gone to his head went instead into the space around the vessels and down into the neck and the chest, and out of the wound. Not all at once. Most of it stayed inside him. That is why the ground is not as marked as you thought it would be, and why the wound looks the size it does. The killing was done inside, where you cannot see it." She held Del's eyes. "The brain went without blood. That is why he stood for one breath and did not speak. He was not choosing silence. He had no blood to speak with. Then he had none to stand with. The going to his knees was the body failing, not a decision. The rolling to the right side was the same. By the time he was on the ground he was, I believe, already past knowing. The heart kept on for a little after. That does not signify either."

The dried cuff pulled at her wrist when she breathed. She let it.

"That is what the blade did. It severed the artery and opened the vein in the right side of his neck, at the level of the angle of the jaw, and he died of the brain losing its blood. Not the wound. Not the steel. The loss." She inclined her head very slightly. "I have said the same thing four times now in four different ways, and it has not changed, and it will not change if you ask a fifth. But I will say it a fifth time if you ask. I have no other appointment on this ground, and I have found that the number of times a man needs to hear a thing is not mine to decide for him."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren looked to the edge of the ground. Two of the witnesses had stopped there when the cart came into hearing, and stood now with their backs to the road and their faces toward the pair of them, waiting to see whether they were wanted. The third had gone. Two would serve. Two had always served.

She did not raise her hand to hold them. They had held themselves.

"You are asking for all of it," she said, "and I am going to tell you a thing first that you will not want, and then I am going to give you what you asked for."

She waited until he was looking at her and not at the ground.

"There is no more. I have not been keeping any of it back. I have given you the place and the depth and the angle, and what the steel did inside him, and how long he stood, and what he did not do while he stood. I have given it in four pieces because you asked in four pieces. You are asking now for the whole, and I will give you the whole, but the whole is not larger than the pieces. It is only the pieces set end to end." Her voice did not change. "If you have been waiting for the part I have not said yet, it does not exist. I would rather you hear that from me now than go looking for it for the rest of your life."

The cart had stopped somewhere past the trees. The men in it would wait. They always waited until the ground was quiet.

"All of it, then. From the beginning to the end, once, as one thing."

She set her feet.

"He came onto the ground correctly and saluted correctly and I returned it. First exchange: he tested my measure and I gave him nothing, and I saw the foot. Second exchange: he tested it again and pressed a little, and I saw the foot again, and knew it was his and not the morning's. Third exchange: he offered the high cut. I did not take it. He recovered with his weight already set and his left foot still coming, and I stepped inside and put the point beneath the right angle of his jaw, upward, two inches and something more, through the artery and the vein together, and it stopped short of the spine, and I drew it out.

"He stood for one breath. I counted it. His eyes were on my face. He did not put his hand to his neck. He did not look toward you. He did not speak, because the blood that speaking runs on was already leaving his head, and by the end of that breath his eyes were not on anything. He did not say a word from the salute to the end. Not one. I would give it to you if there were one. There is not.

"He went down onto his knees and then over onto his right side. It was not a fall. It was the body setting itself down because nothing was holding it up. There was blood at the mouth, a little, not much, because the wound drained inward and not up. His eyes stayed open. There was no sound from him after he was on the ground. There was no movement of the hands. There was the chest, working, for a few moments more, and then not, and the last of it was a shallow thing and it did not look like struggle. It looked like a man finishing a breath he had already begun.

"From the point entering to the standing ending, one breath. From the standing ending to the ground, the time it takes to kneel and lie down. From the ground to the chest stopping, I would say a count of ten, and I am less certain of that than of the rest, because I had my blade to attend to and I did not count it. From the salute to the chest stopping, the whole of it, I would say less time than the account I have just given you has taken to say."

She was silent for a moment. The two at the edge of the ground had not moved.

"That is all of it. Beginning, middle, end. What he said, which was nothing. How long he took, which was not long. What it looked like at the end, which was a man lying on his side with his eyes open and then a man who had stopped breathing, and very little between the two." She looked at him steadily. "It is small. I know it is small. Everything you were braced to hear, everything you have been asking around the edges of, it is not there, because he was not there long enough for it to happen to him. That is the thing the code makes me tell you, and it is the thing that will be hardest to carry, and it is also the mercy. They are the same thing. I have never found a way to hand one over without the other."

She let her hands rest. The cuff pulled at her wrist.

"I have nothing else. Not withheld. Nothing. If you ask again I will say it again, and it will be the same, and you will know then that it is the same because it is true and not because I am tired." She inclined her head, once. "Those two have stayed to hear it. They have heard it. They will say so, if it is ever asked."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Auren heard him confirm it, and heard what his voice did, and did not look away from him while it did it. That was not kindness. It was only that a man who had held his eyes open through the account was owed the same when he closed it, and she had never yet let a second speak the last words to the side of her face.

"Heard," she said. "And witnessed, while there were witnesses. It will stand."

The cart came out from the trees. Two men and a mule, and a board across the bed, and a length of plain cloth folded on the board. They knew the ground. They stopped the mule short of the mark and came on foot, and the older of the two stopped again at the edge and looked not at the body and not at Del but at her, standing on the grass three paces off.

"Who has the account?" he said.

It was their right. She had never known a bearer who did not ask it, and never known one who lifted a man without it. They would carry him through a village and put him in the ground, and they would be asked, and they would need to be able to say. That was not the code. The code was finished. It was older than the code, or beside it, and she had never once refused it.

"I have it," she said. "It has been spoken to his second and to three witnesses, and his second has confirmed it. I will give it to you whole, once, and you will have it as they have it."

The bearer nodded and took off his cap. The younger one did the same, late, watching him.

Auren did not step back onto the mark. She spoke from where she stood.

"He came onto the ground at the appointed hour. He saluted correctly and I returned it correctly. First exchange: he tested my measure and I gave him nothing. I saw in that exchange that his left foot was late on the recovery, that he set his weight before the step was finished. Second exchange: he pressed a little and I still gave him nothing, and I saw the foot again, and knew it for a habit and not for an accident of the morning. Third exchange: he offered a high cut, meaning to draw my guard up and disengage under it to the body. I did not take the cut. On his recovery his weight was already forward and his left foot was still coming. I stepped inside his line and put the point in beneath the right angle of his jaw, above where the collar sits, angled upward toward the base of the skull. Two inches. A little more. It went through the skin and the thin muscle beneath it and into the sheath where the great vessels of the neck run together, and it cut the artery across and opened the vein beside it, and it stopped in the muscle at the back before it reached the spine. It did not enter the throat. It did not come out anywhere. There was one wound. I felt the point stop, and I withdrew it.

"He stood for one breath after the steel came out. I counted it. His eyes were on my face for that breath. He did not put his hand to the wound. He did not turn to look for his second. He did not speak. He did not speak from the salute to the end, not one word, and I would give it if there were one. There is not. By the end of that breath his eyes were on nothing. The blood that should have gone to his head had gone into the neck and the chest instead, and the knowing left him with it.

"He went down onto his knees and from his knees onto his right side. It was not a fall. It was the body setting itself down. There was a little blood at the mouth, not much, because the wound drained inward and not up. His eyes stayed open. His hands did not move after he was down. His chest worked for a count of perhaps ten, and I am less certain of that count than of the rest, because I was seeing to my blade and did not give it the whole of my attention. The last breath was shallow and it did not look like struggle. Then there was none.

"From the point entering to the end of his standing, one breath. From standing to the ground, the time it takes to kneel and lie down. From the ground to the chest stopping, ten, or near it. From the salute to the last of him, the whole of it, less time than this account has taken to say. I do not claim there was no pain. I will not, because I cannot know it. I say that he did not linger, because lingering is a thing I could have seen, and I did not see it.

"I saw the fault in his foot before I used it. I waited for it. I did not make the opening. I found it, and I had been looking for it since the first exchange. If I had taken the high cut he would have lived through the third exchange, and I believe I would have found the same fault in a later one. That is my judgement and I give it as judgement. His hands were good. His measure was good. It was the foot, and only the foot.

"That is the wound and that is the death. His second has heard it and confirmed it. Three witnesses heard it given. You have it now as they have it, and you may say so to anyone who asks you, and you may say that Auren gave it, and you may say where I was standing when I did."

She stopped. The older bearer put his cap back on.

"Heard," he said, and the younger one said it after him, and they went onto the mark and unfolded the cloth.

Auren did not watch them do the lifting. She watched the road, where the two witnesses had already gone out of sight, and she listened to the sound of it, which was a sound she knew, and she did not turn back until the board was in the cart and the cloth was over him and the mule had taken the first step.

The cart went into the trees. The ground was empty. The mark was still there, and the dark place on it that was smaller than anyone would believe, and the two of them on either side of it, and nothing else.

"That is the last time it will be spoken on this ground," she said. "It will be spoken elsewhere. Not by me." She looked at him once more, plainly, without holding it. "You have my name. You do not have to want it."

She turned then, and went, and did not look at her sleeve until she was out of his sight.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway kept the lamp steady, but her gaze did not stay on the shape for long. She looked at the water around it instead, at the way the silt had not clouded properly, at the wet mark on the wall, at the hands buried with such deliberate grip.

“Recently?” she said. “No.”

She let the word sit there, flat and unkind.

“Recently dead things are honest in the worst ways. They bloat, they slip, they give up their weight to the water. They don’t hold a pose. They don’t choose a corner.” Her eyes narrowed a little. “That’s not floating. That’s stationed.”

The lamplight caught one curve of what might have been a skull, or might have been a stone worn into a skull’s idea.

“As for whether it was a person,” she said, “there’s enough of the pattern to make your eyes lie to you. Head where a head ought to be. Arms where arms go. But look at the shoulder line. Too low. And the neck’s got too much length in it, or too little need.”

A dry breath moved through her nose.

“A person has joints because a person has reasons to bend. That thing’s got conveniences.”

She did not smile this time.

“It might have been one, once. Or it might have worn one long enough to keep the outline. Either way, don’t do it the favor of calling it a man. Sentiment makes people reach, and reaching gets them drowned.”

Her thumb tightened slightly on the lamp handle.

“If you need a word for it, call it a latch. Something shaped like a body, put where a body shouldn’t be, holding something shut.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway’s eyes dropped to the water around Pike’s legs, and her expression went very still.

“Plainly,” she said, “you’re standing in the same basin it chose, so keep that lamp steady and don’t kick the silt.”

She did not wait for an answer. She used the better light the way a clerk uses a ledger, moving it over the shape in short, economical passes.

“It came down here before the water settled the way it is now,” she said. “Either it came on its own, or it was put here while it could still take orders. No drag marks on the stair wall. No scrape on the corner where it would have fought. It went to that place and set itself.”

Her gaze marked the silt again.

“It put its hands down first. That’s the important part. A falling body lands soft parts first. A drowning body claws upward. This one planted. It took hold of something under the floor and made its weight into a seal.”

A thin breath left her.

“Then it stopped being alive without letting go.”

She let that sit in the cellar air.

“Death loosens things. Fear loosens them faster. Whatever happened to it, the end didn’t open its hands. The end made the grip more permanent. The bones changed around the posture. The neck stretched because it needed to reach, or because the thing that owned it didn’t care what a neck was for. The shoulders dropped because the arms became the purpose.”

Her mouth twisted, not with amusement but with the old, tired habit of it.

“So plainly: it was used. Maybe it volunteered. More likely it was chosen. Someone needed a lock that looked enough like a person to fool the dark, and they put it here to keep something under the floor from noticing it had been missed.”

She lifted the lamp just enough to show the high stain on the wall.

“That mark isn’t from it climbing out. It’s from whatever pressed against the seal when the water rose. The thing in the silt took the pressure and held. It may have been dead by then. It may have been halfway into something else. Doesn’t matter to the job. What matters is it didn’t move.”

Her voice stayed level, the way one keeps a blade level when scraping wax off a seal.

“What happened to it? It was made into furniture. A doorstop for a bad idea. If there was a person in there once, the person ended when the holding began. The rest is just architecture with teeth.”

She looked back to the curled hands.

“We don’t ask it for its story. We find out what it’s holding, and then we decide whether the world is safer with the story still under the floor.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not soften it. She looked at the shape in the water the way she might have looked at a failed bridge: not with pity, only with the need to know where the strain had gone.

“Exactly is a luxury we don’t get from four feet of black water,” she said. “But I’ll give you what the evidence says.”

She lifted the lamp a fraction, not closer, only enough to let the light define the edges.

“It didn’t break in through wounds. See the jaw? It’s low, but not dislocated in the way a blow would do. The throat’s drawn inward, not out. Whatever took him came down the wet way—mouth, nose, the soft places where a body still thinks it can take in air. It filled the chest first. That’s why the shoulders dropped. The lungs didn’t fail. They were replaced.”

Her eyes moved along the line of the neck.

“Under the skin, there isn’t meat left in any honest sense. The skin’s still there, but it’s been made into a bag. What’s beneath it is strung tight. Corded. Like soaked rope worked through the old channels where muscle used to be. No fat. No give. The veins are collapsed, or full of silt. If you cut it, you wouldn’t get blood. You’d get water, grit, and something fibrous pulling away from the blade.”

She paused just long enough to make certain the thing in the silt was not moving.

“It took the parts that make a person soft. The lungs. The tongue. The eyes. Not necessarily in that order. It took the warmth, because there’s no decay; whatever’s in there has been packed, not rotted. It took the face’s meaning last, I’d guess. That’s the part that lets survivors make mistakes.”

The lamp stayed steady in her hand.

“The neck lengthened because the bones were separated and filled with whatever now runs through it. Black thread, root-work, silt made into sinew—call it what you like. It doesn’t bend like a neck. It extends like a tether. The shoulders aren’t shoulders anymore. They’re anchor points. The arms became the main structure. Everything else is just there to keep the arms in position.”

Her gaze settled on the buried hands.

“The hands are the finished work. The fingers didn’t curl around the floor. They were worked into it. The nails are gone, or drawn back under the skin, because nails are for scratching and tearing, and this thing needed grip without slip. The knuckles are heaped with mud because the hands pushed down until the silt had to make room. If the bones broke, they broke into better shapes for holding.”

A thin, humorless breath left her.

“How far did it get? All the way through. It didn’t wear him like a coat. It used him like a nail. It reached the point where the body wasn’t a person anymore, but a posture. After that, the old man—if there was one—wasn’t suffering. Suffering needs a body that still argues. This one had been edited.”

She finally looked away from the shape, but only to the wet mark on the wall.

“If you meet another one, don’t look for the face. Look at the hands first. If they’re open, it may be dead. If they’re set, it’s working. Look at the joints. If they bend because they must, it’s a corpse. If they bend because it is convenient, you’ve found the same kind of thing. Listen to the water. If it’s noisy, ordinary, stupid with movement, you may still have time. If it’s quiet because it’s waiting, leave.”

Her voice stayed flat, clinical, stripped of any comfort.

“And if you have to touch one—don’t. But if some fool puts a blade into it, expect no blood, no scream, and no surprise. It will use the opening you give it. That’s what it took from him last: the ability to be opened without consequence.”

rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren did not blink, nor did she question the demand. If the second called for the account to be sealed between them—man to man, apart from the arbiters’ ears—then the code permitted no shortcuts, no weariness, and no pity. 

She drew a single, measured breath of the cold morning air, her posture stiffening back into the rigid line of the formal ledger.

"A single thrust," Auren said, her voice dropping into the steady, flat cadence of an oath. "Depth of four inches, struck three inches below the left clavicle. Trajectory downward through the intercostal space, piercing the pleura, the upper lobe of the lung, and the subclavian artery. He did not drown in his own blood; the vessel emptied into the chest cavity before it could rise to the throat. His consciousness ended within four seconds. His heart ceased within eight."

She kept her eyes locked on Del’s, uncompromising and stark. 

"Delivered by my hand, under the third condition of the duel, with steel of regulation length. The grievance is settled. The body is yielded to the second. The account is eleven, and the tally is closed."

She lowered her chin by a fraction of an inch—the prescribed bow of a victor yielding the field to the keeper of the dead—and stood motionless, waiting for the release.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren lifted her right hand, curling her thumb and last two fingers in, leaving the first two straight. She did not point at the man on the grass. She brought the fingers to her own chest, pressing them firmly into the wool of her doublet.

"Here," she said. 

The pressure of her fingers did not waver. 

"Three finger-widths below the collarbone, two inches left of the sternum. The point took him through the third button of his waistcoat—the horn one, carved with the crossed pikes. It split the button in half before it met the cloth."

Her eyes remained fixed on Del's, unblinking, granting no shelter from the fact. 

"The entry was clean. The blade did not catch on the rib; it passed between the second and third. When I drew the steel back, the tip came out red to the fourth inch, grease and dark blood on the fuller. If you strip his linen when the cart arrives, you will find a slit no wider than your thumb, rimmed in blue where the hilt bruised him as it seated."

She dropped her hand back to her side, the fingers resting against the seam of her trousers. 

"Is that plain enough, Del, or do you need me to count the threads?"

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren did not blink. If Del wanted the butcher’s ledger, the code had words for that, too. She had not survived eleven tallies by pretending steel was an abstraction.

"It met three layers of wool, one of unbleached linen, and parted the skin without drag," she said. Her voice was flat, stripped of rhythm, dropping into the cold, technical cadences of a surgeon at an autopsy. "The diamond cross-section sheared the intercostal muscle between the second and third ribs. There was a give in the steel—a pop in the pommel against my palm—when the point pierced the parietal pleura, like parchment tearing under a dull quill."

She took half a step forward, closing the space between them until the smell of the damp earth and the iron stench of the cooling blood rose up between their coats.

"The blade entered the apex of the left lung. It did not tear; it parted the spongy tissue three inches deep. Then the bevel caught the subclavian artery against the curve of the first rib and split the wall lengthwise. It did not nick it. It opened the lumen."

Her eyes held Del’s, wide and dark, unsparing.

"The blood did not fountain onto the grass because the wound channel was plugged by the width of my ricasso until I withdrew. It emptied inward, under four pounds of pressure, flooding the pleural cavity and collapsing the lung from the outside in. His brain starved of pressure before his next breath could draw. The blade took his balance, took the tension in his fingers, and unstrung the sinews in his neck. When I pulled the steel out, the suction in his chest gave a wet cough, and the weight of him fell forward onto the point’s shadow."

She did not draw back. She stood there, her breathing even, letting the butcher’s weight of the accounting sit in the cold air between them.

"The steel destroyed two ounces of muscle, two inches of artery, and the upper third of his lung," Auren said. "It reduced a man who could parry in sixte to thirty pounds of spilled fluid and a dead weight for the timber cart. That is what the blade did. That is what it was done to."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
She straightened where she stood and faced the witnesses fully. She clasped her hands before her to keep them still, and she kept her voice level and loud enough to carry to the farthest of them.

She said, "The account is this. On the third exchange my point entered the left side between the second and third ribs. It passed through the lung and severed the great vessel beneath. The wound was mortal as it was given, and death was not prolonged by the withdrawal."

She did not lower her gaze while she spoke, and she did not soften a word of it, because softening it would have been a dishonour. She had given this accounting eleven times before this day and had taken no pleasure in it then, and she took none in it now. She remained standing when she had finished.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren did not blink. She did not sigh, nor did she look away to the road where the cart was coming. If the second invoked the full clause—the *plenum compotum*—she was bound by the oath she had sworn at eighteen to render every scrap of the dying.

She turned her eyes down to the grass, fixing them upon the dead man's face, and spoke without inflection.

"From the withdrawal of the steel to the cessation of all motor function was seven seconds," she said. "He did not make a speech. Men with an empty vessel and a flooded chest do not compose farewells."

She took one slow pace nearer the body, pointing down with her chin.

"When the point cleared his doublet, he took half a breath through his teeth. It caught in his throat. He made one sound—a hard consonant, a *t* or a *d*, like he meant to say 'turn' or 'don't'—but there was no air behind it to finish the syllable. It came out as a click of the tongue against the palate, followed by a wet whistle through the hole in his wool."

Her voice remained steady, a flat stone falling into deep water.

"His knees gave first, buckling inward toward each other. His right hand remained locked on his hilt so hard the knuckles were gray; the reflex did not release until two seconds after his chest hit the clover. His face did not show pain. The loss of blood to the brainstem produces an instantaneous stupor. What was on his face was confusion—his brow furrowed, his eyes darting toward the hedge as if he believed someone had struck him from behind."

She looked back up, fixing Del with that cold, unsparing gaze.

"Then the pallor took him. The blood drained from his lips first, then his ears, turning the flesh to the shade of tallow or spoiled lard. His pupils blew wide, black to the rims, drowning the hazel in his iris. At the fifth second, his diaphragm heaved once—a dry heave, fighting for vacuum. At the seventh, his lower jaw fell slack, his neck lengthened, and the contents of his bladder released into his breeches. You will smell that when you lift him."

Auren folded her arms behind her back, standing square upon the chalk line, leaving nothing obscured, nothing polished, and nothing spared.

"That is the whole of it," she said. "The seconds, the sound, and the carcass. Write it down or carry it in your skull, Del, but that is how he died."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Auren did not wait for the teamster to lay his hands upon the wool of the dead man’s coat. The code admitted no work upon the field while the final entry hung incomplete between the steel and the ink.

She stepped back to the exact mark where her rear heel had rested at the opening measure. She placed her boots at right angles upon the bruised clover, left heel to right instep, hands falling behind the small of her back. Her shoulders settled into the flat plane of the regulation stance, her head held level, her eyes fixed three inches above the dead man’s brow.

When she spoke, her voice took the high, carrying pitch required by the assize—unhurried, barren of inflection, each syllable dropped like an iron weight into the cold morning.

"Let the book receive the account of the eleventh kill," Auren said. "Struck under the Accord of the Three Bells, upon the lower common of St. Jude-in-the-Fen, before accredited arbiters and the sworn second.

"The engagement opened upon the third stroke of the bell. The steel employed: thirty-four inches of diamond-ground blade, regulation hilt, straight quillons, balanced two inches forward of the shell. 

"The first pass was met in prime; distance kept. The second pass was a disengage into the low line; parried clean with the true edge. Upon the third pass, the deceased suffered a loss of footing with the rear heel, breaking his measure. In lieu of recovery to the guard, he chose to force the line from compromised balance. Upon the fourth pass, he launched a flanconade without opposition, overextending the high line and clearing his chest of steel.

"The strike was mine, delivered upon the lunge, direct, without feint or bind.

"The point took the deceased through the third button of his outer doublet—carved horn, crossed pikes—splitting the horn into two fragments. It parted three plies of wool broadcloth and one ply of raw flax linen without snagging. Entry was effected between the second and third ribs on the left side, two inches lateral to the sternum, three finger-widths below the clavicle. The diamond cross-section severed the intercostal muscle and perforated the parietal pleura.

"The path of the steel was angled twelve degrees downward and four degrees medial. It entered the superior lobe of the left lung to a depth of three inches, parting the spongy parenchymal tissue without resistance. The bevel met the subclavian artery against the margin of the first rib, splitting the vessel longitudinally along its anterior wall. 

"The ricasso plugged the external wound channel during the strike. Upon the withdrawal of the point, three ounces of mixed dark and aerated blood were expelled by residual thoracic pressure, producing a distinct suction at the aperture. The balance of the hemothorax—estimated at three imperial pints—flooded the left pleural cavity, causing immediate pulmonary collapse and catastrophic loss of vascular pressure to the carotid trunk.

"The blade was free of the body at the count of one. 

"At the count of two, the deceased attempted speech, emitting a single unvoiced lingual stop through the teeth, followed by an escape of air through the entrance wound. 

"At the count of three, the knees buckled inward and the trunk rotated forward, the right hand retaining its grip upon the crossguard by involuntary spasm. 

"At the count of four, loss of cerebral perfusion resulted in total flaccidity of the facial musculature and lateral wandering of the gaze, with the irises dilating to the margin of the sclera. 

"At the count of five, the trunk met the turf. The spasm in the fingers released. 

"At the count of six, the deceased exhibited a single diaphragmatic contraction without inspiration. 

"At the count of seven, the sphincters of the lower bowel and bladder relaxed. 

"At the count of eight, all peripheral pulse ceased. 

"The kill was clean, struck inside the circle, without foul or grievance unreckoned. The body is surrendered to the second for carriage. The blade has been wiped. The wood has received the notch. The account is eleven, and the tally is closed before the sun."

Auren ceased speaking. The air hung between them, white with the frost of her breath, until the last vibration of her voice died against the frozen hedge. She remained motionless upon her heels, chin held high, eyes level, waiting for the dead man's keeper to speak the release.

rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
"It is spoken," Auren said, and gave the formula back the way it had been given to her, clean and without decoration. "It stands as the record. The measure is closed."

Behind her the witnesses began to move, slowly at first, then with the ordinary haste of men who had somewhere else to be. The servant's broom started up again on the far side of the yard. Auren listened to both and thought that this was the part no one wrote down — the part where the world simply resumed, indifferent, and the dead man became an errand.

"Vahl's blade goes with the body," she said. "His mother will ask who holds it and where it lies now. You'll answer that honestly, even if the answer is ugly. Especially then."

She shrugged into her coat, which had been hanging long enough to take the cold of the wall, and settled it on her shoulders like something she had worn a thousand times, because she had.

"The cloth burns tonight. The body goes before dark. I'll be at the inn past the mill, and I'll be there till they've had their say." A pause. "Eleven," she said again, quieter this time, and the number sat in her the way a stone sits in a pocket — carried, not shown. She had never once said it as though it were a thing to be proud of, and she did not now.

She walked to the gate without looking back at the body, because the account had already done the looking, and there was nothing left in that yard that belonged to her.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren stopped on the road.

She stood with her back to the gate and let the question stand, because it was a fair question and she had known it was fair when she walked away from it — which was the reason she had walked away from it.

Then she turned and put her hand to the gate a third time and pushed it open. The servant had stopped sweeping again. Two witnesses were still at the wall. It would have to be enough.

"Precisely, then," she said, and set her right hand flat on her left shoulder, above the cut, and spoke in the register the account used and nothing else.

"Vahl's point drew from the seam of the shoulder outward and down, the length of a hand, on a line that followed the slope of the deltoid. It opened the skin and the fat beneath it and stopped at the muscle without cutting the muscle. The vessel it crossed was small. It bled freely, which a shallow cut will do, and more than its size warranted, which is why the coat carries what it carries. The wound is the coat's source. It is not the coat's business."

She took her hand down.

"That is the wound. What I gave you first was the coat's account of the wound. I said *shallow*, and I said *nothing that needs a surgeon*. Both true, neither precise. I was telling you what to think of the blood instead of telling you what the blade did. That was mine to give cleanly, and I gave it soft."

She looked at Del across the yard.

"Twice today. Noted the second time as well."

A pause, and then, flat, with no heat in it and nothing underneath it either:

"Now it is finished. And if you find a third, say it before I reach the road. I would rather stand at this gate until dark than be caught from behind it twice in one afternoon."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren stopped on the road with her back to the gate. The question had gone through the wood and found her, and it was a plain question, and it was owed a plain answer — the account was not complete without it, and she had known it was not complete when she left the yard, which was why she had been walking faster than the distance required.

She turned, put her hand back on the gate, and pushed it open again. The witnesses had not all gone. Two of them were still at the wall, and the servant had stopped sweeping again, and that was enough — enough to speak it in front of, which was the requirement, and she had nearly walked away from a requirement, which sat badly in her.

"Vahl's blade," she said, from the threshold, in the voice she used for the account and not the voice she used for anything else. "He held it in the high guard through the opening exchange. At the turn he brought it down across his body and it passed my shoulder — here—" she touched her left shoulder with two fingers, at the seam, where the coat had a fresh cut in it that the coat had not been given by anyone else "—and carried past. He lost the point of it on the way. It struck the stone of the well-head behind me, edge-first, and turned in the air. It came to rest on the flagstones two paces from the well, hilt toward the wall, point toward the yard gate."

She let that stand a moment, because the witnesses would be picturing it, and they were owed the moment to do it.

"It lies where it fell. I did not touch it. It goes with the body to his family, in the state it fell, and whoever picks it up first should know the edge took a chip at the well-head, a hand's width down from the point. His mother will ask whether the blade failed him. Tell her it did not. It was never given the chance to."

She looked at Del across the yard, still in the doorway, still holding the wrapped blade and the cloth.

"Now it's finished," she said. "That was mine to say and I said it late. Don't make me say it twice."

rows.reply:
Auren's brow furrowed slightly, a hint of frustration flashing in her eyes. She turned back to face the gathered witnesses, her voice crisp and unyielding. "The account has already been given, and the matter is settled. I have no further words to add."

Auren did not turn away. The scabbard hung at her side, and her hand rested near it without touching it again.

“The account is asked,” she said. “It has already been given before these witnesses, but if the second’s voice must call it forward in due form, I will not fault the order.”

She lifted her chin, not in pride, but as one who was about to place a weight where it belonged.

“Let it be heard in full. The challenge was lawful. The ground was set. The terms were named and accepted. No advantage was taken outside the line, and no blow was struck after the halt was called.”

Her voice remained level, stripped of ornament, as though each word had been measured against the dead.

“In the fourth exchange, my opponent received the killing wound. The point entered below the left ribs and passed upward through the body. It reached the heart’s region. Death followed within three breaths. There was no second cut. No further injury was offered. The fall came from the wound alone.”

Auren let the silence hold for the space the code demanded.

“This is the eleventh account I have spoken,” she said then, quieter, but no less exact. “I have never made one of them fairer than it was. What happened here was lawful, not clean. It was within the code, not beyond it. Let the witnesses attest as much, and let no one shape the telling into boast.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren answered without looking away, because the question was proper and deserved no evasion.

“Below the left ribs,” she said. “Not high on the chest, not near the shoulder. The point entered beneath the lower edge of the rib cage, toward the front of the body.”

She lifted her hand once, not to mimic the strike, but to mark the place with the same cold exactness she would have given a map.

“The angle was upward and inward. It did not glance. It did not stop at flesh. It passed deep enough to reach the region of the heart. That was the killing wound. No other blow decided the matter.”

Her hand lowered again.

“If the record must be plain, let it say this: the wound was in the body, not the back. It was received in the exchange, not after. It was mortal at once, and death came before any other injury could be given.”

Auren’s voice remained steady, though steadiness did not mean ease.

“That is where it landed. That is what the witnesses must attest.”

rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren did not look away from the question. She gave it the same weight she would have given a point of order in the line.

“The code names the account of the killing wound,” she said. “It does not ask for the dying to be made into a scene. But if you require all that can be attested, so that no later tongue may fill the gaps with lies, I will give it.”

She stood straighter, not with pride, but with the effort of holding memory to its exact shape.

“He took three breaths after the point entered. The first was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant one, it did not reach speech.”

Her voice did not soften, and it did not harden. It remained true.

“His sword fell before he did. He did not reach for me. He bent toward the wound, then his knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes stayed open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing. The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. There was no spurting that I could attest. There was no long struggle. One small movement passed through him as the breath failed, and then there was none.”

Auren let the silence stand for the space the account required.

“That is how long he took: three breaths. That is what he said: nothing that could be heard as speech. That is what it looked like at the end: a man mortally wounded in the line, going down without insult and without a second blow. Let the clerk write that, if all of it must be written. Let no one add that he begged, or that I watched with pleasure, or that the death was cleaner than it was.”

She turned again toward the clerk’s table.

“I will sign it plain,” she said. “Plain is the only mercy the code allows me.”

Auren remained standing at the clerk’s table, her hands clear of the parchment and the pen. When the confirmation had been given, she did not receive it as comfort, nor did she allow it to become a reason to soften anything that had just been set down.

She looked instead at the clerk, and then at whatever witnesses still remained near enough to hear.

“Let the confirmation be entered,” she said. “But let it come after the account, not in place of it. If the record is to stand, it must stand entire.”

Her voice did not rise. It took on the same measured weight it had carried before, exact and unadorned, as though the repetition were not a burden but a duty.

“Let it be written and heard in full,” Auren said. “The duel was joined before witnesses under agreed terms. The ground was set. The line was marked. The terms were named and accepted by both parties. The signal was given. No advantage was taken outside the line. No blow was struck after the signal to halt had been given.”

The clerk’s pen hovered, then moved.

“In the fourth exchange,” Auren continued, “I gave the killing wound. It was a thrust, not a cut. The point entered the front of my opponent’s body below the left ribs, beneath the lower edge of the rib cage. Its course was upward and inward. It did not glance from bone. It did not stop in the outer flesh. It passed into the body’s inner cavity and reached the region of the heart. The wound was mortal at once.”

She let the words settle, but she did not look away.

“Death followed within three breaths. The first breath was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant any of these, it did not reach speech.”

The scratching of the pen was thin and dry beneath her voice.

“His sword fell before he did,” Auren said. “He did not reach for me. He bent toward the wound. His knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes remained open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing. The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. I will not attest to spurting, because I did not see it. I will not name vessels divided, because I did not open him after death and the code does not require me to feign a surgeon’s knowledge.”

Her face remained austere, but there was no cruelty in the precision.

“There was no second wound,” she said. “No further injury was offered after the fall. No blow was given once the duel was decided. The ground took my opponent, not I. What was done was done in the line, under the code, and not beyond it.”

Auren’s gaze shifted briefly to the parchment, then back to the clerk.

“Let the account also say that the wound was spoken aloud before witnesses, as the code requires. Let it say that the account was asked for and accepted by the second. Let it say that no dishonour was added to the death. Let it say that the dead man’s name stands in the record, and that my name stands beside it, not above it. If there is a line for the victor, let it say only that I remained standing and gave the account. Let no title of honour be added where the code asks for fact.”

She drew a slow breath, steady but not easy.

“If any word has been softened, let it be corrected now. Not *struck*, but *entered*. Not *blow*, but *thrust*. Not *near the heart*, but *reached the region of the heart*. Not *soon after*, but *within three breaths*. Not *expired*, but *died*. Not *the duel ended*, but *death followed*. The code does not ask for pleasant language. It asks for truth.”

Auren’s hand rested briefly near her scabbard, then fell away again.

“This is the eleventh account I have spoken,” she said. “I have not made this one fairer than it was. I will not call it clean. It was lawful. That is all the code permits me to say. Let no later telling shape the matter into boast, or into a tale that spares the hearer what was seen.”

Her eyes remained fixed on the record, as though the ink itself were still answerable to her.

“That is the account,” Auren said. “Let it stand entire, without softening, without omission, without pride.”

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren received the correction as she received all corrections under the code: without resentment, and without the comfort of vagueness.

“Then let it be written precisely,” she said. “The blade made one thrust, not a cut. The point entered the front of my opponent’s body below the left ribs, beneath the lower edge of the rib cage. It passed upward and inward. It did not glance from bone. It did not stop in the outer flesh. It entered the body’s inner cavity and reached the region of the heart.”

She drew no breath for effect; she only made certain the words were complete.

“What the blade did was this: it pierced. It opened a single mortal passage. It caused death within three breaths. What it did it to: the living body of the man named in the challenge, in the front, below the left ribs, upward toward the heart. I will not say which vessels were divided, because I did not open him after death and the code does not ask me to feign a surgeon’s knowledge. I can say the wound was mortal at once, and that no second wound followed it.”

Her hand remained still at her side.

“If the clerk wants the plainest form, let him write: the point entered below the left ribs and killed him. If he wants the full account, let him write what I have said, and let him leave no room for a kinder reading.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge leaned forward, elbows on knees, and looked at the man the way she looked at a map.

"All right. First — the color. Look at his face and then look at the inside of his lip. I do lips and eyelids, because faces lie. A man goes white from fear and it means nothing. But pull the lip down and it's pale as the inside of your wrist — that's blood loss talking, and it doesn't lie." She did it, gently, with a thumb. "See? Pale but not grey. Pale is *low*. Grey is *going*. Grey means the blood that's left has stopped being interested in the face, and it's keeping it for the heart instead. The body's a miser at the end. It knows what it can't replace."

She let the lip go and pointed at the chest, rising and falling under the blanket.

"Breathing. Twenty-something a minute is a man working hard. Fine. Thirty and shallow, like he's taking little tastes of air — that's the start of sliding. And count it steady, not when you remember. It drifts slow and you'll miss the drift if you're only glancing."

She moved her finger to the bandage at the left shoulder, not touching it.

"Seepage is normal. A wound weeps — that's it doing its ugly work. What's not normal is seepage that keeps coming fresh, red and thin, soaking through in minutes. That's a vessel I missed, and it won't stop on its own." Her mouth went flat again. "And the sweet smell. You'll think I'm mad until you smell it. It's not the wound stink everyone knows — that's bad, but bad is honest. Sweet is rot that's gotten ahead of me, and by the time it's sweet, I'm already losing."

She sat back.

"Pulse, breathing, color, bandage. In that order, every time, so you don't skip one because the last one looked fine. It's not medicine. It's a list. Medicine is the list, done when you're tired."

The man muttered something and turned his head toward the lamp, eyes half-open, unfocused.

"He's rousing a little. That's allowed." She watched him a moment. "If he wakes proper, he'll ask three things — water, his arm, and whether anyone saw him cry. You answer the last two honestly and lie about the first."

She looked at Wick, and something in her face eased a fraction, the way a knot eases without coming undone.

"You keep asking real questions instead of comfortable ones. That's rarer than you'd think, and it's the whole job, in the end. The comfortable questions get people buried."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge glanced at the man first — breathing still coming in that same pull-through-the-teeth count, steady enough — and lowered her voice anyway.

"He can hear worse. He owned worse tonight. But sleep is doing him more good than my lecture, so we keep it low." She reached over and took the spent ball off the tray, turned it in the bad light. "All right. Untidied, then. And we'll use him as the lesson, because he got the honest kind, and you should know the dishonest kind before it comes through that flap."

She held the ball up.

"A ball is one story. It goes in the front door and it goes out the back door or it doesn't, and the track between is a corridor you can walk. Everything it did is on that line — that's the tray, that's the whole of it. Shell is two different things wearing one name. Case shot throws balls, and those behave, more or less.

"I plunged the blade into the right shoulder, severing the subclavian artery," she states, her voice as clear and calm as a winter stream. "Blood pulsed out, and he collapsed. Death was swift, from loss of blood and shock."

She meets Del's eyes, a challenge implicit in her steady gaze. The accounting is given, the debt paid. There is no room for sentiment, no need for embellishment. Auren has done her duty, and now it is time to move on. She inclines her head once more, a curt nod of acknowledgement, before turning to leave the courtyard and its grim business behind.

She nodded towards the still form on the ground, her posture unyielding. The accounting had been given, and that was all that mattered. Del's curiosity, while understandable, was irrelevant to the matter at hand. Auren would not indulge it further.
